speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. B. Pearson (Prime Minister):
subtopic: MEDICARE-STATEMENT AS TO IMPLEMENTATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to make a statement on medicare, as I promised to do some days ago.
Early in 1965 the government announced its plan to discuss with the provinces "a way in which federal and provincial action can most effectively contribute to programs that will provide health services to Canadians on a comprehensive basis". At the federal-provincial conference held at Ottawa on July 19, and 20 of that year, 1965, I made it clear that medicare was a matter which required the closest co-operation between federal and provincial authorities. I said then that while the responsibilities of decision and of execution in this matter were essentially provincial, the scope and the nature of the problem was such as to create a national concern, and a measure of federal responsibility.
Today it remains the concern of the federal government to find the best way in which federal and provincial action can most effectively contribute, once the present legislation has come into effect, to achieve a practical medical care program available to as many Canadians as possible and as soon as possible.
[DOT] (2:40 p.m.)
To this end we have consulted the provinces fully at every stage of the development of the medical care program. At the federal-provincial conference to which I have referred, at subsequent federal-provincial meetings of ministers of health, and at a large number of meetings of federal and provincial officials, detailed proposals and arrangements were discussed. Therefore, because of the
February 12, 1968

Implementation of Medicare nature of the issue as well as this requirement of consultation, the government took seriously into account representations made to us recently by the provinces concerning the financial consequences for them in current conditions if they participated in the medicare plan provided for in the legislation passed almost unanimously by the house in December, 1966, and which comes into effect on July 1 of this year.
The situation is that while the benefits of this act are available to any province which wishes and is able to meet the requirements set out in it, only one or two provinces have indicated their intention to come into the program on the date the act comes into effect. The remaining provinces, including the two largest provinces, have indicated that either because of current financial pressures, or of objections to the plan itself, or both, they will not be participating in the national plan at least for the time being.
It is, of course, the responsibility of the provincial governments to decide on financial priorities within their own spheres of operation. Their decisions on medicare made by them in the light of their assessment of the financial situation should be respected and understood.
As a result, on July 1, 1968, when the act comes into effect there will not be anything approaching a universal medicare program in Canada provided jointly by federal-provincial action. A consequence of this is that there will be no significant increase in total financial outlays by the provinces and the federal government for medicare in the next financial year, and nothing to support alarmist and unwarranted statements about the massive and harmful impact of new outlays on financial conditions.
The federal government, while remaining committed to the policy of full medical care coverage for all Canadians, certainly has no wish to bring pressure to bear on provincial governments who, for their own reasons, have decided that full implementation of the medical care program as of July 1 of this year is not in accordance with their own financial priorities.
We shall continue to keep in close touch with the provinces on this subject, and it is our hope that as current financial conditions change, the benefits to Canadians of a full, national medicare program will be achieved through close co-operation between the federal and provincial governments. Indeed, once the act is in effect as of July 1, 1968, it will be


possible to discuss its operation with the provinces, not only in the light of changing economic conditions but also in the light of the experience of its operation in the one or two provinces which came in on the date provided for in the legislation.

speakeroldname: Hon. Robert L. Stanfield (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: MEDICARE-STATEMENT AS TO IMPLEMENTATION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the announcement of the Prime Minister indicating no change with regard to the medicare program comes to me as a great disappointment because I think it represents a grave disservice to Canada.

subtopic: MEDICARE-STATEMENT AS TO IMPLEMENTATION
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: MEDICARE-STATEMENT AS TO IMPLEMENTATION
speechtext:
The government has been urging restraint, has told everybody that it will set a good example and has been urging the provinces to be restrained. The reasons for this, of course, are unprecedented inflation in the country accompanied by a sharply rising cost of living, sharply rising interest rates and a deteriorating competitive position of Canadian producers and manufacturers in world markets as a result of this situation. In addition there has been concern for the Canadian dollar.
In view of the unsettled times in terms of international finance it is surely important that the government of Canada demonstrate to the country and to the world its readiness and the readiness of the Canadian people to make the decisions that are necessary to ensure a strong and growing Canadian economy. Instead of this we have an indication of the willingness of the government to embark upon a vast new spending program, and inviting the provinces to join it. Indeed, this program places a heavy pressure upon the provinces to join in, because the residents of all the provinces will be paying for the program in the provinces which participate in it.
Whatever may have seemed reasonable a couple of years ago when this program was considered by the house is unreasonable today in this regard. A program of this magnitude is obviously completely incompatible With and contrary to the policy of restraint preached by the Minister of Finance. It is bound to increase the difficulties of the government and of the people of Canada, will most probably bring about inappropriate and inflationary measures, and will be interpreted abroad as an act of weakness on the part of the Canadian government. What are we to think of a government which cannot find any money to deal with its own superannuated
February 12, 1968	COMMONS
pensioners, which finds it necessary to welch on commitments already made in connection with manpower training, and yet wishes to embark on this expensive program?
Furthermore, as the Prime Minister has indicated, the majority of the provinces do not want this program in its present form at this time. They may be pressured to join, with the sole result that it will interfere with programs which they consider more urgent, including the training of additional medical personnel so necessary in this country for an effective medical services program.
Despite what the Prime Minister has said, the government has never effectively consulted the provinces of this country on this program. The four basic conditions of the program were imposed and insisted upon by the federal government although the matter is clearly within the provincial jurisdiction. The provinces wanted a more flexible program. Indeed, most provinces questioned the universality of the program.
In nearly every instance the provinces are hard pressed financially to a degree which perhaps few Canadians realize. The government of this country should realize that programs such as the hospital plan and the provinces' own educational programs have a built in cost escalation which is difficult to control. The result is that the provinces are the financial prisoners of programs already adopted. What this program does is to further box them in.
It is folly to say that the provinces do not have to accept the program. The program has meaning as a national program only to the extent that the provinces accept it and proceed with it. Of course a number have already said they cannot join. I do not think they should be pressured to proceed with the program, but the government certainly does that.
[DOT] (2:50 p.m.)
Furthermore, this puts an additional strain on federal-provincial relations. Let us not kid ourselves, Mr. Speaker. We are in for tough days ahead in terms of federal-provincial negotiations. This pretence at consultation and then ignoring what the provinces recommend, going ahead in some provinces when the majority have clearly indicated they do not want the program in this form, is harmful to federal-provincial relations. It is a further strain upon our confederation.
There ought to have been genuine consultation with the provinces, Mr. Speaker. There

This decision announced by the Prime Minister is wrong for the following reasons, amongst others.

I am very glad to have the agreement of hon. gentlemen who are behind the Leader of the Opposition; it shows that he is expressing reactionary ideas that his followers support.
May I say to the Prime Minister, Mr. Speaker, that the difficulties in which Canada now finds itself with regard to medicare are the direct result of the hesitation, the shillyshallying and the lack of courage the government showed when it first introduced this bill. It presented insurance companies and the

medical associations with another year of lobbying all across the country, another year during which they could misrepresent the needs of the people and the facts as they are.
I suggest that nothing contributed so much to the reactions of provincial governments and their supporters than the unjustified and unfounded declaration by the Minister of Finance that what is involved in the medicare scheme is an expenditure of $1 billion. No calculation by any responsible person has gone much beyond $800 million, but the minister made it his business to go as high as he possibly could. I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that the Minister of Finance and perhaps other members of the government have done the best they could during the past year to discourage the provinces from adopting the medicare plan which is now on the statute books.
Some members on both sides of the house have for many years believed that one of the major social measures needed in any civilized community is a medicare plan that is made available as of right to every citizen. Some members of this house have believed that one of the marks of a civilized society is to make certain that no citizen in that society need fear financial disaster following ill health.
When the government brought in this measure, I will be corrected if I am wrong, Mr. Speaker, but as I remember it, with the exception of only very few, the members of Her Majesty's loyal opposition supported the legislation which was at last to give such a plan to Canada. But now, Mr. Speaker, we are told this is not to be the case.

subtopic: MEDICARE-STATEMENT AS TO IMPLEMENTATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson), has just announced that medicare will be implemented on July 1, 1968, if the provinces desire so.
The Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) is rightly concerned about that government statement on the implementation in 1968 of medicare, a plan laid down by the government.
I feel that is an interference in a provincial field, since several provinces have objected and are still objecting to such a scheme, especially Alberta which has a voluntary medical plan and which frowns on any interference of the federal government in a provincial field.
I was listening to the hon. member for York South (Mr. Lewis) who was blaming the leader of the Progressive Conservative party, claiming that they wanted to help and protect large corporations.
Implementation of Medicare
Mr. Speaker, I would point out that in Saskatchewan, when there was a socialist government in power they endeavoured to implement a medicare program on a compulsory basis, but because of the opposition from the medical profession of that province, they were forced to retreat. Such is the result gained by socialism in Saskatchewan. Moreover, it disappeared from that province since then.
Mr. Speaker, the Canadian people need medical insurance; I am convinced of that. But they do not want socialist measures which would impose on them a plan they do not want. That is why we have been suggesting for a long time to the government to consider a group insurance plan open to all Canadians, under which the government would merely guarantee the payment of an initial premium and would leave to the individual the initiative of paying his contribution to the company he chose, if it cost more, he would pay the difference between the government premium and that of the medical insurance of his choice.
Mr. Speaker, respect for the individual is essential in a medicare program and I say that at the present time through its attitude the Liberal government is interfering with individual freedom. The government should study programs which would guarantee to the individual the right to choose the program that suits him. If, until July 1, the government studied various programs, we would not have to follow in the footsteps of Sweden or other communist or socialist countries in Europe. We are able to have a program which can be used as a model by other countries later because we are convinced-and I am convinced-that state socialism is not the answer to our social and economic problems.
The solution, Mr. Speaker, lies in the setting up of a program which will enable each individual to develop freely according to his own aspirations. That is a plan which respects the individual and not a yoke such as the one advocated by the hon. member for York South. He blames those who make profits, but he makes profits in the practice of his profession, and he does not complain about it. Profits stimulate initiative, and in my opinion initiative should be encouraged as much as possible by a responsible government, whether the Ottawa government or that of any other province in Canada.

Mr. Speaker, we have awaited with interest the

February 12, 1968

announcement the Prime Minister made this afternoon about the medical care plan. The Prime Minister said he had no desire to bring pressure to bear on the provinces. I suggest that this is an about face; neither the Prime Minister nor the government took that position when the bill was before the house. In fact the bill was presented with an attitude of "Take it or leave it". No changes to the legislation were contemplated and none were allowed. It was said that the provinces would have a perfect right not to come in; they could exercise their own judgment. Yet the big stick was held over them. If they had their own plans in operation they were told those plans would have to conform with the national plan in order to qualify for the 50 per cent contribution from the federal government.
Many of us supported the legislation although we had serious reservations. We took exception to the compulsory aspect of the medical care plan, to the degree of coverage it provided and to the fact that it was to be administered by a public agency. Despite all representations about these matters the government insisted on putting the legislation through as it stood then.
The Prime Minister, I think, should have discussed with the provincial premiers the possibility of phasing in the program gradually. In that way those in the low income brackets or on pensions would receive coverage and, if it were desirable later, other categories could be phased in as the situation warranted. I believe that this afternoon we might have had a wonderful opportunity to reconsider some of the major issues that were discussed when the bill was before the house. Above all, I think consideration should still be given to the possibility of allowing the existing provincial plans to qualify and be recognized under the national medical care plan.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, members of the house may recall that on June 16, 1967, during the debate on the estimates of the Department of the Registrar General, I indicated that it was my intention to introduce legislation in this session to implement some of the major recommendations of the special committee of the House of Commons on drug cost and prices.
Public concern about this subject has been intense and sustained. There are obvious reasons for this. During any given interval of time, the incidence of disease is far from uniform, and those who pay the largest drug bills are, because of their disability, likely to have incomes substantially below the average. Not only, however, is the incidence of illness in the population uneven, but it is quite unpredictable so that consumers cannot budget for a situation in which they may have to assume the burden of heavy drug costs. Beyond all this, health is naturally a value in
February 12, 1968

Patent Act-Trade Marks Act itself. It is also an important determinant of the productivity of human resources in the economy.
Evidence of the high level of public concern about the supply of drugs in Canada may be found in the number and character of official investigations dealing with the quality, cost and prices of drugs which have taken place.
In 1958, the combines branch began a general inquiry into the manufacture, distribution and sale of drugs following informal complaints about the high cost of drugs. In 1963, after public hearings from coast to coast, the restrictive trade practices commission published its report concerning the manufacture, distribution and sale of drugs.
In 1964, after extensive hearings, the royal commission on health services, commonly known as the Hall commission, published its report which included many recommendations to the government in connection with the drug industry. And finally, last April, after extensive hearings, the special committee of the House of Commons on drug costs and prices presented its final report.
As members are likely aware, similar concern has been demonstrated by government agencies in other countries like the United States and Great Britain.

Mr. Speaker, I want at this stage to extend my own congratulations to the chairman of the House of Commons committee on drug prices, the hon. member for Halton (Mr. Harley), who is sitting in the chamber this afternoon, and the members of his committee who spent many long days and hours reviewing this subject of prime importance to the Canadian people, who gave the situation a thorough review and contributed to public debate and public education on this subject. This committee has reported to the house with many constructive suggestions, some of which are being implemented in the present legislation.

maintopic: PATENT ACT-TRADE MARKS ACT AMENDMENTS RESPECTING IMPORTATION OF PRESCRIPTION DRUGS
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: PATENT ACT-TRADE MARKS ACT AMENDMENTS RESPECTING IMPORTATION OF PRESCRIPTION DRUGS

speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
maintopic: PATENT ACT-TRADE MARKS ACT AMENDMENTS RESPECTING IMPORTATION OF PRESCRIPTION DRUGS
speechtext:
I want to set forth the principles of this bill with some care because of the fundamental importance, I believe, of what I am laying before the house and because of the complicated nature of the legislation. Evidence was put before the Restrictive Trade
Practices Commission and the royal commission on health services, as well as the special committee of the House of Commons, which demonstrated that the price of drugs to consumers in Canada was much higher than comparable prices in most western countries other than the United States.
All three inquiries concluded that Canadian drug prices are unduly high. All agreed that no single measure by itself would bring about a significant reduction in the price that the consumer must pay for drugs, and that a number of co-ordinated steps must be taken.
To illustrate these conclusions I want, first of all, to deal with a number of international comparisons of drug prices. In its report published earlier this year, the special committee of the house indicated that it had decided to assure itself that the situation had remained more or less unchanged since the reports of the Restrictive Trade Practices Commission and the Hall commission. It therefore checked with reliable sources the cost of certain drugs at the retail level in Canada, in the United States and in six European countries. Twelve of the most commonly used and important drugs were selected.
I have in my hand a composite table showing the results of the comparison. If the house would allow me, I prefer not to take up the time of the house to read it but would ask to be allowed to table these figures as an appendix to Hansard.

I should now like to leave the subject of international comparisons of drug prices and turn to other evidence. There is one sector of the drug market in Canada where a greater degree of competition exists. I am speaking of the market provided by hospitals and other institutional buyers such as government agencies. As the special committee of the house pointed out, many hospitals use a type of drug formulary which allows them to buy on a tendering system. In these circumstances the hospital will call for tenders for a particular drug without specifying its brand name. As a result, where there are several companies producing different brands of the same
27053-417J
Patent Act-Trade Marks Act drug they are compelled to reduce their usual price to hospitals if they want to be sure of getting the business.
In its report the Restrictive Trade Practices Commission included evidence supplied by the province of Manitoba in connection with a tender call for drugs for use in mental hospitals in that province. The quotations for equal quantities of the same type of drug showed a variation between high and low bidders of 194 per cent, 221 per cent, 279 per cent and 491 per cent.
Although there is much more evidence, I shall only refer to one other piece of evidence on this subject. Evidence was given to the royal commission on health services that prodnisone, a cortisone preparation used in arthritic and asthmatic conditions, sold for $17 per 100 units to the retail pharmacists in Saskatchewan at the same time that it was being sold at $1.95 per 100 units to hospitals and government departments.
Now I wish to refer to some specific examples which illustrate that there is often little relation between the cost and the selling price of patented drugs. These examples were part of the evidence before the special committee. The first one relates to the drug stelazine. During the inquiry conducted by the combines branch in 1960 the Canadian company concerned was importing stelazine tablets from its parent company in the United States at a laid down cost of $1.32 per 1,000 tablets. The selling price to druggists, deducting the sales tax, was $67.60 cents per 1,000 tablets. Another example was the drug trancopal. The tablets were imported by the Canadian subsidiary at the laid down cost of $3.88 per 1,000. Packaging and other costs amounted to 24 cents, making the total factory cost $4.12. These tablets were sold to druggists at $70.50 and to hospitals at prices ranging from $47.16 to $63.51 depending on the quantity purchased. By the time they reached the consumer these tablets which cost $4.12 already packaged at the factory in final form were sold for $105.
The fact that prices of certain drugs particularly patent drugs, are high is further illustrated by the price declines which occur when a patent expires. There are not too many examples of this because the real drug explosion started with the discovery of the broad spectrum antibiotics in the late 1940's, so that not many patents have expired, the length of the patent being 17 years. The patent for the drug terramycin recently expired in England, and in April, 1966 Imperial

United States prices for Chloromycetin have recently been reduced almost 50 per cent with the expiry of the patent on that drug. These examples demonstrate dramatically the central importance of patents as a factor in the high cost of drugs.
I am not for one moment alleging that the high price of drugs is a result of sinister behaviour by the industry. The drug industry operates within a given economic framework and members of the drug industry, like rational businessmen anywhere, have responded to the profit opportunities provided by that framework. However, I am suggesting that where parliament is not satisfied with the result of operations within a given framework, it is surely up to parliament to alter the ground rules.
Let me take a moment to describe the framework in which the drug industry operates First, the demand for ethical drugs is determined largely by the incidence of sickness and the writing of prescriptions by doctors. Because he must follow the doctor's advice, the patient is unable to purchase any but the specified drug. Ordinarily the busy physician is not price conscious. Often he may not even know the prices of different brands of drugs and therefore he gives the factor of price little consideration when he prescribes a medicine. There is little opportunity for the consumer to switch to something else if he does not like the price. It is true that the consumer could make some savings by shopping around with his prescription, because prices do vary at the retail level. Often, however, quite understandably the worried patient does not do so. More important, as I have said, if the prescription calls for a basically expensive drug, there is nothing the consumer can do about that.
On the supply side of the market, the framework in which the industry operates is such that there are high barriers to the entry of newcomers who might inject new and more vigorous competition by importing the basic drugs for processing and packaging in Canada or by importing dosage forms. The most important of these barriers arise as a result of the interaction of the Patent Act, the Trade Marks Act, the customs tariff, the very intensive and costly program of marketing


and promotion undertaken by the established firms, and the requirements of the Food and Drugs Act.
[DOT] (4:00 p.m.)
It is not surprising in these circumstances that the major drug firms have not on the whole found price competition necessary. In many cases they have been able to use patents to prevent the entry by others into the production of individual drugs. They have substituted for price competition the development of minor differences in the product and vigorous sales promotion of these small differences. They have also used vigorous sales promotion to minimize the impact of such price competition as might be offered by smaller firms. The vast bulk of advertising done by the major firms tends by its sheer magnitude to obscure the very existence of small sellers. In the case of patented drugs, no price competition need ever develop during the life of the patent.
We are now in a position to explain why the level of Canadian drug prices is amongst the highest in the world. Because of the heavily protected position enjoyed by the producers, drug pricing is based chiefly on demand. The policy of charging what the traffic will bear can be followed. This means that drug prices will be the highest in those countries where the per capita income is the highest. This relationship was confirmed by an analysis presented by the Canadian Pharmaceutical Manufacturers Association of Canada to the special committee under the chairmanship of the hon. member for Halton (Mr. Harley). The higher the income, the higher the price that can be obtained.
The alternative explanation that drugs are sold at lower prices in foreign countries because production costs are lower there does not stand up to factual examination. It is quite common to see a drug that is manufactured in the United States and exported to a European country selling much more cheaply in that country than in the United States. Since the demand and supply characteristics of the market tend to rule out price competition in the Canadian drug industry, except in sales to institutions, rivalry between drug firms takes the form of concentration on the development of minor differences in products and of sales promotion. Competition is, therefore, cost increasing. The more intense the competition, the higher costs are driven. Since there are no downward pressures on
February 12, 1963	COMMONS DEBATES	6623
prices, there is no downward pressure on costs. Rivalry between the firms requires more detail men, more advertising and so on. The resulting higher costs are used to justify higher prices. The evidence submitted to the special committee of the house by the Canadian Pharmaceutical Manufacturers Association showed that virtually the same amount was spent by the industry on sales promotion as on manufacturing the product. There were 49 members of the association who employed 1,799 detail men, and the association estimated there was one detail man for every ten physicians in Canada.
It is understandable, therefore, that the special committee of the House of Commons, as well as the other inquiries to which I have referred, came to the conclusion that the funds spent on promotional activity by the industry are excessive. The government now has a program which it calculates will bring about a reduction in the price of drugs to the consumer. The objectives of the government's program are to bring about the reduction in the price of drugs to the consumer by a number of steps which are expected to have a cumulative effect. The steps must be consistent both with the supply to the Canadian market of quality, safe, efficacious drugs in which the medical profession has confidence and with the existence of a viable, competitive Canadian drug industry. The program, therefore, has three objectives: lower prices, safe drugs and a viable domestic drug industry.
The program may be summarized in this way: The first step is the one which the Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp) has already taken in removing the sales tax from drugs and reducing the customs duty from 20 per cent to 15 per cent as well as substantially narrowing the application of the dumping duty to imports of drugs.
The second step is the one we are now bringing before the house. It is proposed to stimulate price competition among sellers of patented and trademarked drugs through reducing protection against imports which is provided by the Patent and Trade Marks Acts.
As a third step, it is proposed that a program be undertaken to provide objective information to the medical profession about the properties and prices of available drugs so that prescribing physicians will be aware of the price differences between competing drug products of demonstrated quality, safety and effectiveness.
Patent Act-Trade Marks Act
Fourth, it is proposed that steps be taken to strengthen the small sector of the industry that manufactures and sells lower price prescription drugs.
Fifth, consultation with the provinces is planned to tackle the problem of reducing the cost of retail distribution of drugs. This subject falls primarily within provincial jurisdiction.
While each element in the program will be effective on its own, Mr. Speaker, no single step by itself can be depended upon to have a substantial effect on prices. These measures are cumulative and we shall therefore be proceeding with the program as a package.
I want to make it clear to the house, sir, why the amendments to the Patent and Trade Marks Acts are in our opinion necessary. The tariff changes announced by the Minister of Finance should assist in stimulating price competition. However, as the law now stands patents may be used as an absolute barrier to imports and thus may frustrate the benefits of tariff reduction. The effect of removing the sales tax could also be frustrated. The special committee of the house concluded that without more effective operation of competitive forces than now exist in the drug industry in Canada, the only certain result of the removal of the sales tax would be a reduction in cost to the manufacturer. In actual fact, most drug producers appear to have passed on the bulk of the sales tax removed, and I am glad to acknowledge this. Unless more real competition can be introduced, we can have no guarantee prices will not move upward again and absorb the tax saving.
As hon. members know, the Patent Act creates a temporary monopoly in the patented product or process for the inventor with the object of encouraging invention, change and innovation and of making the fruits of that invention available in due course to the public at large. The granting of a patent to the inventor or his assignee gives him the power to prevent others from making, using or selling the patented product or process for a certain period of years. Under Canadian law, patents relating to food and drugs have been placed in a special category. In the first place, the act provides that in the case of an invention relating to a substance prepared or manufactured by a chemical process and intended for food or medicine, the patent does not include the product itself unless prepared by the patented process. This is the present law and it has been the law since
$624	COMMONS
Patent Act-Trade Marks Act 1923. Any person, therefore, is free to produce, import and sell the same product as long as it is not made by the patented process.
In the second place, under the present law provision is made for the granting of a compulsory licence of a patent for invention intended for or capable of being used for the production of food or medicine. When an application is made, the commissioner of patents must grant a licence, which is limited to the use of the invention for manufacturing a food or medicine, unless he sees good reason to the contrary. The commissioner, in so doing, fixes the amount of royalties payable by the licensee for the use of the patent, having regard to the desirability of making the food or medicine available to the public at the lowest possible price consistent with giving to the inventor due reward for the research leading to the invention. This is the present law.
The full privileges of patent protection, therefore, have not been granted to drugs. The Canadian Pharmaceutical Manufacturers Association has referred to this as discrimination. I think it is more accurate to suggest that parliament, for over 40 years, has recognized the important principles of public policy involved, has weighed them and has decided that in this particular case the immediate welfare and interest of the general public is paramount and private interests of the industry, as well as whatever inducement to research the patent would represent, are to be subordinated to the public interest.
I think it is worthy of note that less than 5 per cent of the patents granted by Canada on drug processes are issued to residents of this country. Thus the patent system is an expensive way of stimulating inventive activity in Canada. The government can and does provide more direct and effective inducements to research in the form of statutory grants made available through the Department of Industry. These grants are made available only to the firms which are actually willing to do research in Canada. Patents, on the other hand, are given equally to those who are prepared to do research in Canada and those who are not prepared to do such research.
Compulsory licences to manufacture under section 41, subsection 3, of the Patent Act have not been sought in substantial numbers. In many cases it is apparently uneconomic to manufacture in Canada the basic drug to which the patent relates. This is borne out by the fact that the existing firms, including the

DEBATES	February 12, 1968
major international firms, import most of their active ingredients. In fact, it is my information that 85 per cent of the manufacturing in Canada does not relate to the manufacture of the basic chemical or ingredient that goes into the drug but involves the conversion of the basic chemical that is imported into the final dosage form, whether it be a pill, tube, or whatever form it takes, e (4:10 p.m.)
The Pharmaceutical Manufacturers Association of Canada has stated that "it has not proved economically feasible to develop a pharmaceutical chemical industry itself, primarily because of the limited size of the Canadian market." Those words are the association's. I think there are other factors that probably bear on the situation. These include the high promotion costs which would subsequently be entailed, opposition to and appeals against licence applications which would have to be anticipated, and the live and let live attitudes on the part of the established international firms.
It is instructive that compulsory licences have been obtained and exploited chiefly by wholly Canadian firms. The Harley committee found that competition over a wide range of products has not developed through compulsory licences to manufacture. The alternative stimulus to competition, namely, the importation of drugs ranging from the basic chemical to the final dosage form, has not been given an opportunity to work in the Canadian market because the commissioner of patents has held that he is not authorized to issue a compulsory licence for import of a drug under section 41 (3) of the Patent Act. The fundamental purpose of this bill is to amend the Patent Act to provide beyond any doubt that the authority of the commissioner of patents to issue compulsory licences for patented drugs shall extend to the import of drugs in all forms.
I want to make it clear that this is not such a novel or unorthodox proposal as some industry spokesmen would have us believe. First, it is at least arguable in law that the commissioner now has authority to issue compulsory licences for the importation of the active ingredients. The amendment will eliminate any uncertainty in the present law. Second, one of the main recommendations of the royal commission on patents-the Ilsley commission-was that the Patent Act should be amended to prevent patents from being
February 12, 1968	COMMONS
used as a non-tariff barrier to trade. In other words, the Ilsley commission recommended the abolition of patents in so far as those patents acted as a substitute for a tariff. Third, as the special committee of the House of Commons pointed out, the section in the United Kingdom legislation of 1949 which corresponds to our section 41 (3) authorizes compulsory licences for imports, and this fact does not seem to have held back the growth of the British drug companies. Fourth, in the United States in circumstances in which a drug patent covers only the process and not the product made by the process, importation of the product does not constitute infringement.
The special committee of the House of Commons recommended that the commissioner of patents should grant a licence for import only when he considers it is in the public interest to do so. At present the commissioner is required to issue a compulsory licence, as the statute says, "unless he sees good reason to the contrary".
I want to deal with some of the recommendations made by the special committee of the house so as to show where, in certain details, we are departing from those recommendations.
This recommendation of the special committee introduces a new principle which would tend to restrict the issue of licences to import. It would place on the commissioner the difficult burden of determining the public interest. Accordingly, the existing principle of licensing, that is, the issue of a licence unless the commissioner sees good reason to the contrary, will be maintained by the amendment and extended to the compulsory licensing of imports.
Another recommendation of the special committee was that "the patent commissioner, in assessing royalities on the granting of a compulsory licence, shall consider that the patentee who discovers and initially develops the drug in Canada should have higher royalties than the drug manufacturer who discovers new drugs outside Canada". While I have a good deal of sympathy with the purpose of this recommendation, we are unable to adopt it, particularly because discriminatory royalties would be in breach of the Canadian government's obligations under the international patent convention.
Under the United Kingdom legislation the comptroller, in assessing the royalties for a compulsory license, takes into account the
DEBATES	6625
Patent Act-Trade Marks Act patentee's expenditures on research and development and on the promotion of the patented drug. It has been urged that this or a similar formula should be imported into the Canadian legislation. There are a number of compelling arguments against this but to save time I shall mention only three of them.
First, in the United Kingdom the patent is on the product as such, whereas in Canada the patent is on the process, or on the product when made by the patented process. Since the patent does not extend to the drug substance as such in Canada, the key factor being the process, the supreme court has held that the promotion and other costs associated with the finished drug are irrelevant in setting the royalty. It seems obvious that in principle the royalties should be related in some way to the invention, that is, to what is patented. Not only is this logical but it is the established practice in Canada with respect to other industries.
Second, the cost of research, or a contribution with respect thereto, may be recovered not only by royalty payments on the patents but also by the repatriation of profits earned by the Canadian subsidiary. While prices in Canada remain so much higher than they are in many other countries, the argument in favour of an increased research contribution by the Canadian consumer is not persuasive.
Third, the adoption of the principle followed in Britain could frustrate or at least impair the downward pressure on prices we seek to achieve.
The special committee of the House of Commons expressed the opinion that there is no doubt that the manufacturer who introduces a new drug should be allowed a certain time to promote the drug and establish his position in the market following appropriate clinical testing, so that for a period of time at least he retains his monopoly position. However, the new drug regulations of the food and drug directorate in effect provide a monopoly for five years. The committee felt this was an adequate period for recouping a reasonable return on research, and I agree with their view.
The special committee of the House of Commons also expressed the opinion in connection with compulsory licensing that difficulties can be anticipated from artificial delay that may be introduced by the patentee during the course of prosecution of the application which could lengthen enormously
6626	COMMONS
Patent Act-Trade Marks Act the period between the date of application and the date the patent issues. The monetary rewards to a patentee as a result of delay in the compulsory licensing application, the committee said, can be substantial. The special committee therefore recommended an amendment to provide that if the grant of a compulsory licence takes longer than 12 months the commissioner may issue the licence subject to revocation if any appeal against the issue of the licence is upheld. Subsections 5 to 11 inclusive are intended to give effect to the principle which the special committee recommended should be adopted.
The special committee also recommended that the grant of a licence should be subject to a report by the food and drug directorate to the effect that the applicant had satisfied the directorate that he met the regulations under the Food and Drugs Act. However, the food and drug directorate will enforce the regulations relating to safety and quality irrespective of the grant of a licence. The question of safety is therefore more properly left to the food and drug directorate than to the patent commissioner. It is, however, important that the directorate should have early notice of any application for a licence. The commissioner will, therefore, be required to give notice of the application to the food and drug directorate in order that it may take any necessary action. Moreover, the commissioner of patents will be concerned as in the past to screen out fly by night operators and to deal only with responsible applicants.
The special committee also recommended that the rules under the Patent Act be amended to permit the commissioner to seek and receive outside independent expert advice on the matter of the public interest. However, authority to obtain expert evidence already exists under section 4 (2) of the Patent Act. Thus no new provision is required.
The special committee recommended that the importer of drugs under compulsory licence should pay the cost of the food and drug directorate's services outside of Canada made necessary by the proposed import. It is our feeling that this would be discriminatory in that such costs are not borne by the resident manufacturers or by other importers of drugs, whether patented or not. Moreover, it is questionable whether this would be consistent with the GATT and other international trade agreements. It is not, therefore, proposed in this legislation.

The special committee pointed out that under present law the Canadian subsidiary of a foreign parent company can prevent the importation of drugs into Canada if these bear trade marks identical with those owned and used by it. This, of course, rules out imports of brand name drugs which may be selling at lower prices outside Canada and which, in fact, may in many instances be identical with those drugs manufactured by the subsidiary from bulk active ingredients imported from the parent corporation.
The special committee noted that prior to 1953 a trade mark could not be assigned or transferred to another corporation, even a subsidiary corporation, without at the same time transferring the good will of the business. Under the Trade Marks Act, 1953, this situation was reversed and subsidiaries or licensees became legally entitled to use the trade mark of their parent corporation under a "registered user" system. The subsidiary, for example, provided it operated strictly under a registered agreement with its parent corporation, obtained equal rights to the trade mark of the parent.
In representations made to the joint committee, the Patent and Trade Mark Institute of Canada expressed the opinion that if the Canadian company does not own a Canadian registration but merely uses the mark as a "registered user" thereof, the trade mark being actually owned by the foreign related company, sale of the trade marked wares imported from the foreign related company would not constitute an infringement of the registration. It appears, however, that a court decision of 1960, Remington Rand Limited v. Trans-World Metal Company Limited, clearly gives the owner of a Canadian trade mark the right to exclude trade marked goods manufactured by related companies outside Canada.
It is proposed, therefore, to amend the Trade Marks Act to provide that no infringement of a trade mark can be claimed where drugs, bearing the trade mark of and manufactured by a related company in a foreign country, are imported into Canada. This is a recommendation of the special committee of the House of Commons and of the Royal Commission on Health Services. The amendment will apply in the situation where a foreign parent and a Canadian subsidiary sell a particular drug product under the same trade mark both in Canada and in the foreign
February 12, 1988
country. The amendment will permit a third party to import the drug into Canada when it has been manufactured by the foreign parent. It will not allow the importer to abuse the trade mark or deceive customers. Such imports are likely to occur only when the price in Canada is substantially above the price in the foreign country.
At the present time patents may be invoked to prevent the import of patented drugs either in the form of the fine chemicals or in dosage forms. The proposed amendments to the Patent Act will facilitate the import of drugs in the form of fine chemicals. However, the sale of imported dosage forms could still be prevented under the provisions of the Trade Marks Act. In order to facilitate the import of dosage forms it is therefore necessary to adopt both the patent and trade mark proposals.
I want to talk now about the question of quality and safety. As I said earlier, this is of paramount importance to the Canadian public. Assurance of a high level of quality and safety of drugs is of prime importance to the public interest. A patent, however, has nothing whatever to do with quality. We should not confuse the purposes of the Patent Act with the purposes of the Food and Drugs Act. Some industry submissions would have us believe that only a patented or trade marked drug carries the assurance of high quality and safety. This is simply not the case. Assurance of quality depends, first, on the integrity of the particular manufacturer and, second, upon the controls exercised by the food and drug directorate. The patent itself confers no guarantee of quality, nor is it an essential condition of quality. There is no evidence whatever that drugs which have never been patented or on which patents have expired are any less safe than patented drugs.
Under the proposed amendment, where the preparation of the dosage form continues to be carried out in Canada, the situation presents no new elements and therefore no greater difficulties than exist at present. On the other hand, if the drug is imported in final dosage form as a pill, serum or in a tube, evidence must be available to indicate that all requirements of the Food and Drugs Act and regulations have been met. This may entail inspection of the foreign plants in which they are produced. In any instances where these requirements are not met, the product can of course be excluded from the Canadian market, regardless of whether a patent has been granted or license issued.
