The food and drug directorate already has responsibility for all drugs on the Canadian market, including those imported from abroad. To the extent that the program increases the volume of imports, there will be an increase in the work load of the directorate. The problems will, however, differ only in degree, and the directorate believes that, with the additional resources that are being put into place, it can continue to discharge its responsibility in relation to quality and safety.
In its report the special committee said that unfortunately the large international drug manufacturers often give the impression that the products of small drug companies are not safe. This was challenged not only by the small drug manufacturers themselves but also by purchasing agents of some hospitals and government departments who have ordered and continue to order the products of the small companies.

It has to be recognized that no matter how much opportunity for price competition may be opened up, unless the physician has confidence in the manufacturer of the drug and in the measures taken to ensure the purity, safety and effectiveness of the product, he will not prescribe it for his patient. It is, therefore, important that full attention be given to the necessity of building up confidence on the part of physicians in the quality of available competing products. Lacking the time or resources to make a comparison between the properties and prices of competing products, the doctor prescribes those drugs he has heard of, has read of and has some knowledge of. Being a cautious man, he prescribes the drug manufactured by a company known to him. He may or may not know what the drug costs, and he may or may not realize that there are lower cost alternatives on the market.
It is, therefore, essential to the success of the whole program that the physician develop confidence in and prescribe lower-priced drugs when he is satisfied that they will adequately serve the needs of the patient. The special committee of the House of Commons accordingly recommended that the food and drug directorate should publish periodically an informative bulletin to the medical profession with detailed information on drug properties, action and prices. The directorate is making plans to carry out this recommendation.

6628	COMMONS
Patent Act-Trade Marks Act [English]
Within the Canadian drug industry there exists a group of firms whose business consists chiefly of the manufacture of lower priced drugs. This sector comprises over 100 smaller manufacturers, mostly Canadian owned, which together account for only some 15 per cent by value of the market, about $30 million at factory prices.
The dissemination of information on comparative properties and prices, as I have just mentioned, is designed to stimulate the demand for lower priced drugs, including the products which the smaller firms manufacture or are capable of manufacturing. The changes in the anti-dumping regulations and in the Patent Act will also open up additional opportunities to them. However, before they can take full advantage of the new situation it will be necessary for some of them at least to regroup or reorganize into units of greater strength and capability if they are to compete effectively for a significant share of the retail market for their lower-priced drug products. Plans to strengthen the competitive position of this sector of the industry are now under consideration and will be announced in due course.
[DOT] (4:30 p.m.)
While attention in the various studies I have mentioned has been focused on the price of drugs at the manufacturing level, it is widely recognized that a further basic cause of the high price of drugs lies in the high cost of retail distribution. In the submission of the Canadian Pharmaceutical Association Incorporated to the special committee it was stated that in 1964 an average pharmacy dispensed some 30 prescriptions each day of the year, the sales from which represented only 27.4 per cent of the gross sales of the pharmacy. According to the special committee, these figures and others presented to it clearly indicated that the average pharmacist in an average community could not hope to survive unless he also operated his pharmacy as a small goods retail outlet. The special committee concluded there were indications that serious inefficiency existed as a result of too many drug stores serving too few people. It added that inefficiency leads to higher prices.
The special committee also noted that the provincial pharmaceutical associations appear to exercise great control over their pharmacist members through regulations and standards of ethics. In considering what might be

DEBATES	February 12, 1968
accomplished in reducing prices at the drug store level the special committee had to keep in mind the division of powers between the federal and provincial governments. As I have previously told the house, I am planning early visits to the provincial capitals to examine jointly with provincial leaders the problems of the consumer and methods of solving them on a broad base. These visits will, I hope, lead up to and prepare the ground for a federal-provincial conference on consumer affairs. In these discussions the retail distribution of drugs will have a high priority. The federal program which I have been outlining is designed to tackle high drug prices at their origin, that is, at the manufacturers' level. But it is essential, and this is our intention, to initiate action at the level of distribution through discussions with the provinces.
I should like to analyse briefly our reasons for feeling this program will be effective. I believe there are a number of reasons which justify confidence that, taken as a whole, the program I have outlined will be successful in reducing the price of drugs. In the first place, there is overwhelming evidence that there is scope for substantial reductions. I have earlier referred to the fact that many of the international companies operating in Canada sell drugs abroad at much lower prices, and since this is a persistent phenomenon it cannot be argued that this is unprofitable for them. I have referred to the tremendous spread between the manufactured cost of some drug products and the manufacturers' selling price. I have referred to the fact that the selling costs of this industry are as great as its manufacturing costs, and I am not aware of any other important industry where selling costs represent such a high proportion of the final price. I shall refer in a moment to the evidence that profits in the Canadian drug industry have continued year after year at a level twice as high as manufacturing generally.
In the second place, in the one sector of the market where competitive forces are sometimes able to operate, namely, in sales to hospitals and other institutions, some drugs are sold at half the price or less than that charged to the retail trade. In the third place, we know that in other jurisdictions, such as Britain and the United States, when important patents have expired there has been a dramatic fall in prices. In the fourth place, even under the present provisions for compulsory licensing, in the limited number of
February 12, 1968

cases where new producers have been able to enter the market, price reductions have occurred. In the fifth place, while the existing provisions for compulsory licensing have been taken advantage of primarily by small Canadian companies who have selected certain products which it was practicable to manufacture completely in Canada, the possibility of importing the active ingredients under compulsory licence should encourage the small companies to expand their activities substantially. In turn this may induce the large international companies to broaden -heir lines through compulsory licensing in order to preserve their shares of the market. There are indications that some international drug companies are likely to seek compulsory licences to import if these amendments are passed by parliament.
Finally, members must certainly be aware that the industry itself anticipates that these measures will put a substantial downward pressure on prices. For example, in its presentation before the special committee of the House of Commons Hoffmann-La Roche commented: "The mischief for Roche lies not so much in what business would actually be lost to copiers but what happens to the price level as a result of their entry".
Although, as I have indicated, the most important effect of the patent proposals may be to permit importation of the basic chemicals, there will be some products the demand for which will be too small to justify the preparation of dosage forms in Canada. Provision for the importation of drugs in dosage forms is, therefore, important. It is in connection with the possibility of importation of dosage forms that the proposed change in the Trade Marks Act is necessary. Taken together, the patent and trade mark proposals should have the effect of ensuring that prices in Canada are brought more into line with world prices. Importations will occur, however, only to the extent that high prices in Canada make such importations economically feasible. Faced with the likelihood of import competition the established industry can be expected to reduce its prices to avert it.
I should like to consider briefly the impact of these proposals upon the drug industry as we see it. The latest census of manufacturers by the Dominion Bureau of Statistics taken in 1965 lists 162 manufacturers of pharmaceuticals and medicines employing 11,137 persons. Total manufacturing and related operations by themselves accounted for the employment
Patent Act-Trade Marks Act of less than 4,400 persons. Administrative and office employees numbered slightly more than 3,800. There were over 2,800 persons engaged in sales and distribution. The submission by the Alberta government to the special committee pointed out that wages and salaries paid by drug firms represent only about 30 per cent of the value of output, while in most industries it is closer to 70 per cent.
Canadian drug manufacturers both manufacture and import. There is no substantial fine chemicals industry in Canada and the basic drugs are therefore mainly imported. I said the figure was roughly 85 per cent, that is, the percentage of the basic chemicals which is imported. In many cases final dosage forms are also imported by subsidiaries of the manufacturers. The manufacturing activity in Canada is largely a matter of converting bulk drugs into dosage forms and packaging and marketing them.
It is not possible to predict the magnitude of additional imports which may result from the extension of compulsory licensing to cover importation of drugs. Nor can reliable estimates be made of the proportions of these additional imports which will take the form of finished drugs on the one hand and of ingredients on the other.
There is no obvious reason why compulsory licensing of imports should significantly change the present relationship between imports of finished drugs and imports of ingredients. The same amount of manufacturing should continue to be done in Canada though it may be rearranged in terms of the competitive forces involved. At the present time it is more difficult for potential importers to obtain supplies of low-priced dosage forms than it is for them to obtain supplies of low-priced chemicals. The patent and trade mark proposals will not make the availability of low-priced dosage forms any easier. Where the potential importer has access to a supply of low-priced dosage forms, the patent and trade mark proposals will, of course, make it easier for him to sell them on the Canadian market. If importation takes the form of basic chemicals, this will have an effect on those few firms which manufacture such chemicals in Canada but this is a very small segment of the pharmaceutical industry. Such imports cannot substantially affect employment in the drug industry in Canada since at most they will simply result in other firms doing what is being done by the present patent holders. To the extent that this occurs, it will at most shift operations from one plant to another.
February 12, 1968

Patent Act-Trade Marks Act There is every reason to expect that Canadian branches or subsidiaries of large international firms will themselves seek compulsory lincences and begin producing dosage forms of drugs in Canada which they are now precluded from producing because of patent restrictions. This would mean an increase in competition among the large and well established firms. To the extent that some patent holders have in the past imported finished dosage forms rather than basic chemicals, the patent proposals may have a tendency to increase the amount of manufacture in Canada.
While the proposed steps are designed to inject real price competition into the drug field with the expectation that prices of drugs will fall, nevertheless the established firms in the Canadian drug industry will still be afforded substantial protection. This arises out of the 15 per cent m.f.n. tariff, the "new drug" regulations which I shall explain in a moment, the sales promotional activities of the established firms and the remaining patent and trade mark protection.
[DOT] (4:40 p.m.)
We are not abolishing the Trade Marks Act and we are not abolishing the Patent Act. Neither should it be forgotten that the average rate of return on investment over the past 12 years in the Canadian drug industry was 20 per cent for all drug manufacturers compared with about 10 per cent for all manufacturing. There is thus in our opinion a substantial cushion for the established drug firm in adjusting to the new conditions of the market. An appendix to the report of the special committee of the House of Commons points out that during this 12-year period the return on investment to the pharmaceutical industry tended to increase, while the return on investment for all manufacturing showed a substantial decline. Moreover, the committee concluded that contrary to what some have claimed, the financial experience of the Canadian pharmaceutical manufacturing industry does not indicate that business risks to it are greater than to manufacturing in general in this country. On the contrary, said the committee, the evidence indicates that it has been less risky.
I now wish to say a word about the significance of the new drug regulations under the Food and Drugs Act. Before the sale of a new drug is permitted the manufacturer must carry out extensive and very costly tests and
(Mr. Turner.]

submit the results to the food and drug directorate. If the directorate is satisfied as to the safety and efficacy of the drugs on the basis of the evidence submitted, it issues a notice of compliance on the basis of which the drug may be sold by the person or firm who submitted the evidence. The drug remains a new drug until it has been sold in Canada in sufficient quantity and for a sufficient time to ensure that any serious side effects will have shown up. As long as it remains a new drug no other person or firm may sell it unless he has submitted similar evidence to the directorate and received a notice of compliance. In general it is not economically feasible for a second person or firm to duplicate work of the first person or firm and this is not done in practice. A new drug-I emphasize this-usually remains classified as such for a minimum of five years. Hence, in practice the holder of a patent on a new drug enjoys absolute protection for five years. Only when the drug is removed from the new drug classification is the question of compulsory licensing likely to arise.
The special committee of the House of Commons expressed its opinion that the patentee has ample time to establish and consolidate his position in the market and thereby recoup his research costs by virtue of the fact that it takes some five years for the drug to lose its new drug status. It also concluded that it was most unlikely that a compulsory licence would be sought prior to the date that the drug lost its status as a new drug.
In summary, it is to be expected that the major effects of the proposed amendments will be to reduce the prices, selling outlays and profits of existing large drug firms, rather than to decrease greatly their share of the market. Output can be maintained to the extent that they are willing to cut prices to meet the challenge of imports, and this will maintain output and employment in existing plants.
There is one other important consideration relating to the impact on the industry of the proposed amendments to which I should like to devote some attention. In its report the special committee of the House of Commons noted that when the report of the royal commission on health services was written the 13 largest firms in the drug field in Canada, exclusive of Connaught Research Medical Laboratories in Toronto, were with one exception all branches or subsidiaries of foreign firms. Since then the Frosst company
February 12, 1S6E	COMMONS
has been taken over by a United States firm. Since the report was written the last large Canadian firm, in other words, was purchased by a United States corporation.
According to the submission of the Pharmaceutical Manufacturers Association of Canada to the special committee, 36 of its 57 members are based in the United States and many of the rest are based in Europe. As I have mentioned earlier, 95 per cent of all Canadian patents are owned by residents of foreign countries. If anything, the proportion of drug patents held abroad is probably higher than 95 per cent. Given the fact that most of the Canadian drug industry is foreign owned and the fact that most drug patents are foreign owned, the chance of any Canadian firm being able to break into the market on a substantial scale is very limited under present circumstances. The amendments to the Patent Act which have been proposed are likely to be of crucial importance in making entry easier for Canadian owned drug firms.
Spokesmen for the major drug firms often defend the height of their prices, or the gap between computed costs and market prices, by reference to the vast sum spent on research in the interest of advancing the cause of health and medical science. It is also asserted that in the absence of the patent incentive, research would disappear. I should like to say, Mr. Speaker, that 1 believe fundamentally in the importance of research in this country. I have said on many occasions that our research in Canada is less than 1 per cent of our gross national product, whereas in the United States it is 4 per cent or 5 per cent and in the United Kingdom 3 per cent or 4 per cent. But it applies to the international drug industry and the amount of research done in Canada, the statements I recited from the industry should be questioned.
In terms of the manufacturers' sales dollar, as reported by 41 members of the Canadian Pharmaceutical Manufacturers Association for the year 1964, only 7 per cent was spent for research and development of all kinds. This figure included sums charged to the Canadian companies by related companies outside of Canada. At the same time, sales promotion expenses accounted for 30 per cent of the manufacturers' sales dollar. Hence over four times as much was spent on sales promotion as on research. The proportions are not greatly different in the United States.
The 7 per cent research figure takes into account the fact that research spending by
DEBATES	6631
Patent Act-Trade Marks Act the drug companies has been increasing substantially in Canada in recent years. I should like to suggest to the house that this increase cannot, however, be attributed to the operations of the patent system. In its submission to the special committee the Pharmaceutical Manufacturers Association of Canada said that both in Canada and the United States the requirements of government for additional data before a new drug is allowed on the market have sharply increased companies' research and development expenditures. In support of this proposition the association quoted this statement about the United States drug industry:
Industry research people estimate that the cost of developing a new chemical entity has increased somewhere between 20 and 50 per cent in the past few years, with most of the increase due to meeting the requirements of the food and drug administration.
Elsewhere in its brief the Pharmaceutical Manufacturers Association of Canada referred to the increase in research spending between 1959 and 1964 and acknowledged that this expansion was due in part to the research tax incentive offered by the federal government and to the fact that a few companies had been given direct grants for specific projects. The special committee of the House of Commons reached the conclusion that Canada was a late starter in drug research and because of this the international aspect of the drug industry should be studied before any hasty recommendations were made about the promotion of further research in the Canadian branch of the industry. The special committee suggested that any further tax concessions that might be conferred on the Canadian drug industry should be considered in the light of what benefits are likely to be attained from the total package of research and development undertaken. If this examination is not carried out, the special committee suggested, it is conceivable that the taxpayer will be asked to pay for clinical research and testing which are normal expenditures of any industry, and the manufacturers will reap the benefit at the expense of the taxpayers and, I might say, at the expense of the consumer.
It has to be borne in mind that it may well be cheaper for Canadian firms to continue to acquire the result of research by purchasing it abroad, particularly through their parent organizations. The reason why Canadian subsidiaries of international drug companies do not do more research in Canada was explained to the special committee by
February 12, 1968

Patent Act-Trade Marks Act Canadian Cyanamid. It said that Cyanamid's drug research is carried out largely by the thousand scientists and technicians in its New York laboratory. Economic considerations have dictated the concentration of the principal pharmaceutical research effort at a single location because of the heavy investment required in specialist facilities and personnel. The Cyanamid submission argued that it must be obvious that fragmenting such an operation was not feasible. In its report the special committee came to the conclusion that the drug industry in Canada would continue in the foreseeable future to remain largely within the international framework, that the larger Canadian companies would remain subsidiaries of foreign corporations, and that any further noticeable increase in research in Canada by these subsidiaries would in all likelihood not take place unless stimulated by government policy, that is to say, by government grants, tax incentives and the like.
[DOT] (4:50 p.m.)
It is perhaps worth recalling that the Canadian market is of relatively minor importance to anyone wishing to market a new drug discovery. Drug research is predicated on the idea of supplying a new discovery to the world. In logic, therefore, there is no reason the proposed patent amendments should change the locus of any research undertaken which is contemplated, if there are otherwise good economic reasons for locating it in Canada. Of all Canadian subsidiaries of international drug firms only three have done any appreciable research in Canada and this for historical reasons, prior to their purchase by international concerns. Most of the research has been produced on the international scene. I think one should pay tribute to Frosst and Ayerst, McKenna. I do not want in any way to downgrade what they have done for Canadian technology and research. As a matter of fact, the director of research for Ayerst is now rector of the University of Montreal. He is a very distinguished Canadian, indeed.
I have heard much about the argument in respect of exports. The proposed amendment can have no important effect on exports because exports from the Canadian drug industry are not substantial now. The Department of Industry estimates that exports amount to something over 5 per cent of Canadian production. Owing to the structure of the industry and the fact that all important companies are owned abroad, so that potential export markets are served by affiliates


located there or by the parent companies, the likelihood of a substantial export business being developed by the companies most affected by the proposal is remote. This appears to be accepted by the Pharmaceutical Manufacturers' Association of Canada, which said that pharmaceutical companies in Canada have developed primarily to serve the domestic market and few of them export. Conceivably some export business might be developed by truly independent Canadian companies.
The special committee of the House of Commons reached similar conclusions. The Harley committee said that in so far as the export market is concerned, unless the patent owner is Canadian the international patent system can prevent and it does discourage development of the drug industry in Canada. With most foreign owned patents, subsidiary companies of the parent patentee control the market within their own jurisdictions. Export activity must therefore be confined to those areas of the world where patents are not taken out, areas which are relatively and commercially insignificant. The special committee of the house reported that on a question addressed to one Canadian subsidiary of a United States parent corporation the answer was succinctly put, "We have so many plants all over the world I just do not know where we would export to."
I have taken a great deal of the time of the house, and I thank hon. members for their indulgence in hearing me out. I feel this is a complicated and important piece of legislation and that I owed it to members of this house to explain it as fully as I could. In all that I have said I have had in the forefront of my thoughts the essential and important part which drugs play in the health care of the Canadian people. I want to be as categorical about this as it is possible for me to be. There is no issue between myself and spokesmen for the drug industry about the very great benefits that drugs have conferred on Canadians and the very great benefits that the Canadian industry has conferred upon Canadians. Indeed, it is the very importance of drug products which makes the performance of the drug industry so critical. What we do not wish to see is the great benefits flowing from the availability of modern drugs being persistently overshadowed by their high cost to the consumer.
Finally, I wish to refer briefly to what I said during the debate when the consumer
February 12, 1968

affairs bill was before the house last November, and specifically about the importance of having a federal presence in the consumer field. The drug program which I have just outlined is an example of how it may be possible in the future to co-ordinate government policy in the interest of the consumer in a more effective way than has been done in the past. The fact that there is now a minister responsible for this function should make it possible to seek out other ways by which the federal government can assist in reducing prices or restraining price increases in areas of vital concern to consumers in spite of the fact that we have no direct constitutional authority to impose control over prices or wages.
I shall conclude my remarks by reminding the house that it is now over four years since the report of the first major inquiry into the drug industry was published-not since it was begun, but since it was published. It may have been worth waiting for the findings of the Royal Commission on Health Services and of the special committee of the house on drug costs and prices in order to ensure that the most careful consideration was given to the issues involved. These amendments are a direct result of the review by the special committee of this house under the chairmanship of the hon. member for Halton. I believe the time has come when the public is looking to parliament for effective action.

maintopic: PATENT ACT-TRADE MARKS ACT AMENDMENTS RESPECTING IMPORTATION OF PRESCRIPTION DRUGS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to congratulate the minister on his marathon speech and for recognizing that this is a complex piece of legislation, bad in respect of some points, which he did his best to dress up and gild. It has a great many loopholes and I intend to deal with some of them, particularly those in respect of patents and safety which he passed over so easily.
Bill C-190 is intended to increase price competition among pharmaceutical manufacturers in Canada by depriving them of the limited patent rights they own on certain processes for making drugs they have invented. Canadian patent rights on prescription drugs are already weak in comparison with those of other countries. Under existing Canadian legislation there is a legal procedure known as compulsory licensing. It works in this way. Company A, after long and expensive research, invents a drug and obtains a patent to process and manufacture it. Immediately it is granted a patent, Company B may apply for a compulsory licence enabling it to use the same process patented by company A.

Patent Act-Trade Marks Act This licence forcibly deprives company A of the full benefits of its own invention. Such a licence is granted to company B almost as a matter of right for a royalty which the commissioner of patents himself has described as a mere pittance. Company B must make the drug in Canada.
The patent amendments now proposed will remove this requirement in respect of manufacture in Canada. They would extend the grounds for granting a compulsory licence so that prescription medicines produced outside the controls provided by the Canadian Food and Drugs Act could be imported into Canada. The changes proposed to the Trade Marks Act would permit the importation into Canada of drug products manufactured by a company abroad under the same trade mark used by the related Canadian company. This would permit the false assumption that drug products bearing the same trade mark would be identical in all countries.
This bill virtually abolishes patent protection for drugs and amounts to discriminatory confiscation of property without any compensation whatsoever and without any guarantee of the intended public benefit. The public did not need this bureaucratic bill from the mushrooming department of the new minister.
Bill C-190 deals with patent rights which are perhaps moral and economic issues. Fundamentally, putting the matter in its most simple form, a man or a woman spends days, months or years working hard and long to develop an idea into something tangible. It matters not whether the idea relates to a drug, a food or an implement. Surely that person should not be cheated of the rewards of his labour either in part or in whole. This is the moral issue involved in removing or restricting patent rights. It goes beyond cheating a person out of his ingenuity; it discourages incentive and invention. It discourages research and destroys industry. People struggle and work in their own laboratories or in company or university laboratories, unseen, largely unhonoured and unsung, many of them reaping little in the way of monetary return. Out of 3,000 experiments, approximately only one comes through and produces a useful drug. Therefore a man could work in research all his life and never come up with a worth-while finding.
[DOT] (5:00 p.m.)
I think back to the early 1920's when Banting and Best worked in a small laboratory in
February 12, 1968

Patent Act-Trade Marks Act Toronto-coming from that area and knowing both of them I am very cognizant of this -under the direction of Professor MacLeod, a Scotsman, head of the department of physiology of the University of Toronto. There was at that time no drug treatment for diabetes; it was a hopeless condition. Juveniles, young adolescents and middle-aged people died long before their time. Juvenile diabetics died within a few years. It was a pitiful thing. I remember one young person 18 years old dying in something like a period of two months. The economic loss was measured in millions and millions of dollars. This, then, was the situation when Banting and Best undertook their experiment which had been tried in 1896, about 27 years earlier-I think this illustrates the whole problem that the minister did not grasp-by Claude Bernard and was unsuccessful. Research is a long, continuing process.
Why did Banting and Best go into this endeavour? Banting was a medical doctor, raised in Alliston, Ontario, a short distance from where I practise. I knew him very well. During his high school years he was very distressed by a young girl whom he saw daily becoming thinner and thinner and wasting away until she died. This had a profound impression on this young high school student and was the main reason Banting went into medicine and research.
There was here the dedication and incentive to produce a material that would cure or arrest this disease. Banting and Best were able to produce insulin which controled diabetes. I had just graduated from medical school when that happened. In 1926 we were just starting to use the fruits of their labour. Insulin has been improved over the years and has rescued millions of people from an early death. In dollars and cents, Mr. Speaker, insulin has rewarded the world economically by billions of dollars to say nothing about preventing untold suffering. Brilliant scientists, with their diabetes under control, have carried on their life's work and added to the storehouse of knowledge of the world. I know two from the University of Toronto who have done so. People of all vocations suffering from diabetes were able, generally speaking, to live out their life span and work at their calling.
The world rejoiced when insulin was discovered at the University of Toronto. The minister talked about this young country not being able to keep up in respect of research. May I remind him of the fact that at that time


there were only 10 million people in Canada. When the great discovery of insulin was made the world rejoiced. This demonstrates beyond peradventure the point that research can be carried out successfully in a small country.
The patent rights to insulin were turned over by Drs. Banting and Best to the governors of the University of Toronto. Over the years the returns from those patent rights, placed in a trust fund, have largely financed the Connaught Laboratories. Perhaps it would be in order to refer to Dr. J. K. W. Ferguson, one of the outstanding physiologists in the world today and director of Connaught Laboratories. Dr. Ferguson says on this subject:
.. .it has undoubtedly been drawn to the attention of the government that virtual abolition of patent protection for the drug industry in Canada would be disastrous for the prospects of developing a competent, research-oriented drug industry in Canada.
This information paper published by the University of Toronto goes on to state:
What does not seem to have been pointed out yet is that other countries may be pressed to take retaliatory action against Canadian exports, if the Canadian subsidiaries of their companies have been subject to confiscation of an important commercial asset.
The brief advances the opinion that all drugs in Canada are not overpriced and the number that are overpriced at the retail level may be very small. It proposes that, in the interest of obtaining well-informed and fair-minded opinions, data on retail drug prices be sent to the Canadian Medical Association with the request that they be studied by its committee on pharmacy and such other expert opinion as they consider desirable.
I noted that the minister referred to doctors being so busy that they did not know just what they were using in the way of drugs. I do not know whether that is what he meant but that is the impression he gave me. The minister can correct me if I am wrong. Doctors may write prescriptions for all the drugs used in Canada today, and I certainly hope they are not only conscious of the drug they are using and the job it will do but are also thinking of the patient and the price of the drug. I believe this is true of at least 90 per cent of the doctors in our hospitals. They certainly know the qualities of different drugs because they are using them by their generic names. Those drugs have been proven clinically, which is a different situation from the
February 12, 1968

one to which the minister was referring. I continue quoting from this paper:
Dr. Ferguson recalls that the Connaught Medical Research Laboratories were set up by the University of Toronto "for the purpose of research in hygiene and preventive medicine and the preparation of serum and vaccines or such other substances as may hereafter be found to be useful in the prevention of disease ..."
From the earliest days, the laboratories have been essentially self-supporting from the sale of products and earnings have been kept by the governors in a trust fund for the support of medical research and for the capital expansion of the laboratories from time to time. Over a period of 50 years, they have grown to the point-
This started with the humble beginnings of the discovery of insulin by Drs. Banting and Best in a very small and inadequate laboratory judged by today's standards.
-where they now employ 730 persons and total sales fluctuate between $6 million and $7.5 million per annum, of which between $1 million and $1.5 million have been in the export market. The laboratories spend $1.4 million to $1.7 million on research each year.
The minister knows as well as I do, and I am not going to embarrass him by saying it, how little money goes into medical research in this country. The minister knows this because he quoted the figures of one to five compared with the United States. The minister has the figures and knows this. I want to compliment him on dressing this bill up in the way he did, knowing the facts, the weak points and the holes in it.

The Connaught Medical Research Laboratories have made many important contributions, in addition to the mass production of insulin. The first introduction of this continent of toxoid for protection against diptheria was achieved by the laboratories during the late 1920's and early 1930's. The introduction of combined immunizing agents against diptheria, tetanus and whooping cough followed during world war II. The first full-scale production of heparin, a widely used anti-clotting agent, was developed during the mid-1930's. About that time, the first large scale production of crystalline insulin was also accomplished. The formula for tissue culture medium 199, which made the development of Salk vaccine possible, was published by the laboratories in 1949 and methods for large scale production of polio virus were pioneered. It is likely, in fact, that this very important development innovation would have been an ignominious failure without C.M.R.L.'s contribution.
The contributions of the Connaught Medical Research Laboratories to preventive medicine are by no means at an end. Several expensive projects currently under development include a new and safer vaccine for the prevention of rabies, a vaccine to prevent german measles, and an enzyme to dissolve blood clots.
Anyone with friends or relatives who have had rabies vaccine administered to them knows that its effects are severe and that it is not without fatal dangers. At the present time the laboratory is working on a vaccine which may restore life to some Canadians.
The brief continues:
Each of these absorbs some hundreds of thousands of dollars over many years before it can earn any return, the brief points out. A long period of substantial profit is therefore essential if expenditures of this magnitude are to be amortized.
"It is a real question whether such profits could be achieved without patent protection in Canada", asserts the brief. "They certainly could not, without patent protection in other countries."
What I shall read now will demonstrate how far the minister has strayed from the Harley report. The brief continues:
Commenting on the possible effects of the 23 recommendations of the special committee on drug prices, the C.M.R.L. brief states that none of them would affect the financial interests of the laboratories to any significant extent. It goes on to say, however, that "in recent weeks, newspapers have quoted cabinet ministers as forecasting drastic action to reduce the duration of patents on drugs to two years. In addition, there have been less definite forecasts of changes in the law of trade marks as they apply to drugs.
This illustrates and demonstrates the necessity for patent rights if research is to be carried on and if the benefits of that research are to be passed on to mankind.

Patent Act-Trade Marks Act Mr. David Henry, Q.C., an honoured member of the civil service patent branch, has stated that the reasons for the high prices of drugs are not singular but multiple. I do not think the minister grasped the significance of that statement. They are multiple and they relate not just to the pharmaceutical manufacturing industry but to retail pharmacies as well and, indeed, to the taxation policies of the government, to the food and drug directorate through the regulations it imposes on industry, to the drug wholesaler, to the physician who prescribes the drugs, and to the consumer himself who demands the very best care for himself and his family. If Mr. Henry is able to say that the bill before us could destroy the drug industry, and he indicated it might, is it not peculiar that the Department of Industry has not looked into or given any advice on this matter? Has the minister consulted the Department of Industry on it? Here we have an industry that, according to my figures which vary from those of the minister who said a lot without substance and said it well, employs 10,000 people in Canada, 2,500 of whom are highly trained individuals. The minister and I will have to get together and compare our sources of information. The associated drug services encompass another 25,000 people. This bill means that we would lose 2,500 scientists and then the others would follow them.
Pharmaceutical research costs approximately $12 million annually. The minister said we need more research in this field and he quoted figures to back his statement. I agree with him. The federal government has done nothing to increase this sum except to allocate certain amounts to medical research. I want to compliment the government for allocating some money for this purpose.
The policy of the government seems to offer no protection to an industry which could well become a major industry in this country and which started as did Banting and Best who began research on dogs in a little room and whose association developed into the large industry of which I spoke. The government has adopted the same policy with regard to the drug industry as it does with regard to other industry by allowing imports to come into Canada from countries where labour costs are half what they are in Canada or less and whose productivity is just about
[Mr. Eynard.l
as good as ours. I might also mention the textile industry. No provision has been made to protect that industry when the Kennedy round tariffs come into effect on July 1. The United States textile industry could dump a sufficient amount of its products in Canada in one lot to ruin our small textile industries. I do not know whether the government has taken or contemplates any measures to protect this industry. If they have they should let us know because questions have been asked on this matter. The same situation exists with respect to the boot and shoe industry. I am referring to these industries because they are affected by economic factors and they are in the same situation as the drug industry.
[DOT] (5:20 p.m.)
What has the government done? Unemployment has risen sharply. The boot and shoe industry is the biggest labour employer in Canada; yet the government has done nothing to protect it from increasing foreign imports. All one has to do is take a good look at the record. I am disturbed about these conditions because I have a shoe industry in my riding as well as a textile industry. They are both seriously disturbed about the attitude of the government. Now the drug industry will be in the same position, but I hope we will be able to convince the government they are on the wrong course. The minister has hopes in so far as April is concerned. Perhaps he can be the young Lochinvar who can change this picture and start the government off on the right path.
The other day the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Winters) indicated he was not going to protect the fruit and vegetable growers of western Ontario. He said they would have to be competitive with producers who are paying less than one-third the wages our people are paying. What does he want to do to our standard of living? What does he want to do to the Canadian people? It is time we took a good look at some of the things this government is doing. There are 77,000 more unemployed, the government is hurting the footwear industry, the textile industry, the drug industry and the farmers. What will be next?
I have mentioned these points in relation to our economy because they are of concern to every man and woman across Canada. If we achieve cheaper drugs of poor quality we could destroy the industry in this country. I want the minister to pay attention to this. Bill No. C-190 fails to reflect the urgent safety
February 12, 1968

requirements recommended by the Harley committee. Safety must be paramount. A compulsory licence to import drugs must not be granted until the food and drug directorate has inspected the manufacturing facilities in the country of origin. How is the minister going to accomplish that, Mr. Speaker? These manufacturers should meet the same standards as are set for Canadian drug manufacturers. How are you going to get permission to do that? One could conclude from the minister's remarks that everything was all right if one did not know that is not the case. He put a very good face on it and said everything would be inspected. How much money has he provided for new inspectors or other officials who are going to be needed in the food and drug directorate? I should like the minister to tell me that. If money has been set aside, it must be hidden. Of course, this government has hidden many things, but so far as the house is aware not a solitary thing has been done about it.
The minister stood up and presented a bad case very well. He told us he was going to send inspectors all over the country. He had lots of them. The Canadian people could be sure of the safety and quality of the drugs used. I am hoping that after some consideration the minister will come back tomorrow and tell us he does not have these men and did not mean his remarks to be interpreted that way. After all, he is a nice fellow. The minister put on the record some of the things that have been accomplished in so far as cutting the cost of drugs is concerned. I believe he would like to give everybody credit for what is being done, so I am bringing this to the minister's attention. I do not want what he said here today to be the cause of any ill will by not recognizing what has been done.
The druggists across Canada have tackled this situation. In my own town druggists have started charging a prescription fee in order to reduce the price of drugs. Prices have been reduced to such an extent that the other day I calculated that a drug which would have cost $15 under the old system now costs $8. The druggists have helped to put their house in order. The pharmaceutical firms have been putting their house in order. They have been cutting down on their commission men and putting them on salary in order to cut costs. This is one good thing the Harley committee has accomplished. It has made people think about what we can do.
Patent Act-Trade Marks Act
Above all, we must be Canadian. We must keep things Canadian. We must support research. We must do things that will develop Canadian industry and enable it to compete anywhere in the world. I could refer to Toronto University, Connaught laboratories, Best, Banting, and so on. I could put other names on the record. What has the government done? I do not want to embarrass the minister, but what has he done to provide these inspectors who are to do all this checking? Dr. Chapman gave evidence to the committee that the department was busy now and he did not think they could do more than they are doing. I am sure he is right. What has the government done? Industry has done something and the druggists have made a contribution.
The minister drew attention to the hospitals, and I am glad he did. Le me tell him something about hospitals. They do use these drugs, but they only use drugs that have been clinically tested and which they know are going to produce results. The hospitals have a pharmaceutical committee to protect them but there is no such protection for the public outside. The sad thing is that the hospitals under the jurisdiction of the Department of National Health and Welfare buy drugs and the people prescribing them do not even know where those drugs come from. Did the minister know that? If he checks the evidence he will find this is so. However, all the witnesses were asked if the drug were to be used on their wives or families which one would they prefer and they all answered, a brand name drug or a proven clinically tested drug.
I am putting these facts on the record because the most important factor is quality.
There is one other thing I want to say to the minister because he is not in this business and probably does not know about drugs and how they act. The minister talked about the quality and safety of drugs or I would not have mentioned this. The minister referred to Chloromycetin from which patent protection was removed and the price went down. Does the minister know that the United States has had to give Parke Davis exclusive patents rights again? If I remember correctly, a few weeks ago I was told in the United States that five drug firms had obtained the right to manufacture Chloromycetin or chlorman-phenical. This drug went into hospitals in the United States. Hospital after hospital reported they were not getting results with the Chloromycetin made by the other five drug firms.

Patent Act-Trade Marks Act They discovered that the blood levels were down and that the drug was not having the desired therapeutic effect. It was not doing what the doctors expected it to do. So bad was the situation, Mr. Speaker, that the licences of the other five firms producing the drug were cancelled. So I draw to the attention of the minister that the situation is not quite as simple as he pretends it is.
[DOT] (5:30 p.m.)
If I may go back to the recommendations of the Harley committee, Mr. Speaker, they recommended as a statutory requirement that the granting of a forced licence be subject to a report by the food and drug directorate of the Department of National Health and Welfare to the effect that the applicant for the compulsory licence has satisfied the directorate that he has met the regulations under the Food and Drugs Act. I did not hear the minister state that even this nominal safety provision had been included. I should like him to tell the members of the house when he replies whether it has been included.
In similar circumstances, where the product in question is no longer a new drug the directorate has simply certified that the firm has adequate manufacturing facilities and controls and complies with section C.01.052 of the regulations. This relates only to the manufacturing facilities and has nothing to do with purity or equivalency of the product in question. Under present regulations there is no way that the safety recommendations of the Hilliard committee can be implemented with regard to drug licensing. As I understand it, Mr. Speaker, this point was paramount in the consideration of the commitee. Perhaps it is why the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs does not want to interfere with the statutory prerogative of the patent commissioner. The special committee considered this matter as well but stated that the safety factor is of such importance that the food and drug directorate should participate in the disposition of applications relating to compulsory licences.
With regard to imports, the parliamentary committee felt that safety must be paramount. A compulsory licence to import must not be granted except where the food and drug directorate has inspected to its satisfaction the manufacturing facilities in the country of origin, and in accordance with the same regulations that pertain to Canadian drug manufacturers. None of this has been
[Mr. Rynard.l
DEBATES	February 12, 1988
provided in the present legislation. The minister will undoubtedly state that safety provisions are not a proper requirement for the Patent Act. I should like the minister to give some explanation of this. Be that as it may, Bill C-190 clearly directs the commissioner as to when and under what circumstances he shall grant a licence, and it should, therefore, provide the commissioner with proper guidance in the determination of the drug safety provisions for such licensing.
Bill C-190 does not discriminate between the two types of compulsory licensing as clearly recommended by the parliamentary committee. In the case of compulsory licences to import the commissioner should only grant the licence if in his discretion it is in the public interest to do so. The public interest would be, the committee feels, the need to bring lower drug prices to the consumer weighed against the effect of such import licence on the Canadian producers of the drug in question. The differentiation between the two types of compulsory licensing should be carefully observed. It must be obvious that one of the effects that such importation would have on the Canadian producer would be to weaken his control of quality of the drug product in distribution-the minister spoke about this this afternoon-and economically limit the extent and type of medical and technical support services provided the medical profession.
Perhaps the more basic intent of the minister's department is illustrated best in the legislative interpretation of Harley committee recommendation No. 20, which is as follows:
__if the granting of a compulsory licence takes
longer than 12 months, the commissioner, if in his opinion the delay is unwarranted, may toe empowered to issue the licence subject to revocation if any appeal against such a compulsory licence is upheld, providing however that such licensee provide sufficient evidence to satisfy standards of the food and drug directorate.
Bill C-190 essentially instructs the commissioner to issue interim licences only after six months and ignores reference to the food and drug directorate or any consideration of needless delay. Certainly that is my interpretation.
It should hardly need repeating that safety must be paramount. It is dangerous to implement only the licensing recommendations of the parliamentary committee without also enforcing the urgent safety and equivalency requirements of this same committee and those of the Hilliard and Boyd expert committees.
February 12, 1968

The second recommendation made by the special committee reads as follows:
That the personnel and facilities of the food and drug directorate be expanded to make possible the implementation of the recommendations of the Boyd committee, the Hilliard committee and this committee.
Needless to say, Mr. Speaker, we are fully sympathetic with the intent of the legislation but, as noted before, we cannot support a bill that does not provide the essential safety and equivalency requirements recommended by the special committee of the House of Commons on drug costs and prices.
If the question is one of quality drugs at a fair and reasonable price versus unknown or inadequate drug products at the cheapest possible price, then our answer must be "no" to Bill C-190. If the consensus is that quality drugs cost more than necessary, then we should be exploring means to negotiate an equitable price without destroying the technical-medical base of the Canadian drug industry.
A Canadian manufacturer cannot meet the prices of Italian or similar competition as long as he continues to conduct essential and expensive research in this country, as long as he manufactures to Canadian standards in Canadian factories, employing Canadian labour at Canadian wage rates, as long as substantial costs are required to service medically Canadian and export markets in a technically competitive industry, and as long as he is paying over 50 per cent of his profits to the government in the form of income taxes alone. Perhaps the minister has forgotten that.
It is in this spirit, Mr. Speaker, that we intend to move a number of amendments to the bill. This bill is both complex and complicated. The minister himself spoke for almost two hours and I have spoken for far too long. I was glad to listen to what the minister had to say and I think he did a terrific job on an impossible bill. He put many things on the record with which I did not agree and which when subjected to the cold glare of examination just do not stand up. Nevertheless this is an important bill, and I would suggest to the minister that it be sent to a committee so it can go over some of the points that are giving us trouble.
I should like to sum up, Mr. Speaker, by saying that quality and safety must be the overriding factors when considering price. Patent protection for inventors is a basic
Patent Act-Trade Marks Act principle of justice that is recognized by civilized nations and is the most important incentive for industrial research today in this country. Compulsory licensing can only be based safely on yet to be established criteria for the therapeutic equivalency of generic counterparts. Forced licensing of imports without such safety and clinical assurances will dangerously debase the quality of presently available drugs, destroy drug research and manufacturing in Canada and undermine Canada's international reputation with respect to the recognition of scientific and industrial property rights. And I do not think the minister wants to do that.
[DOT] (5:40 p.m.)
The proposed Patent Act changes must be urgently reviewed with relation to the yet to be implemented safety and equivalency recommendations of the Hilliard and Boyd reports of 1955 and 1956. Also, the Economic Council of Canada's present over-all review of industrial patents must be considered. The minister did not even wait for that review. I do not know why because he has a high regard for the Economic Council of Canada.
I had hoped that this matter might be referred to a committee. I submit that drug prices can be equitably negotiated without destroying the technical and medical base of Canadian industry. Neither society's demand for new drugs nor Canada's need for an international competitive research capability will be satisfied by those who would inadequately copy the discoveries of others and market them solely on the basis of price under the protection of forced licences. I submit that ultimate economies and increased benefits to Canada's society will be obtained through the discovery of new and more effective drug products.
In conclusion, may I again urge the minister to send this matter to a committee so that we may consider it once more. This is a most important bill. If I have been critical it is only because I want to be helpful and to bring out all factors. I hope the bill will be referred to a committee so that essential points may be discussed in order that we may build a bigger and better Canada.

Mr. Speaker, I shall begin my remarks by reading a few words:
The manufacture and distribution of medicines, because of their intimate relation to the health
February 12, 1968

Patent Act

Trade Marks Act and welfare of a community or nation, partake of the nature of public utilities. In view of the shifting of control from professional to financial hands, manifested by recent developments in the drug industry, the public interest may require "regulation" of the industry, through the guarantee of a fair return to investors and the limitation of prices to be charged to consumers.
That was a quotation, Mr. Speaker, from a book entitled "The Costs of Medicines" by C. Rufus Rorem and R. P. Fischelis, written in 1932. It goes to show that in those days, 36 years ago, someone foresaw what would happen today. Now we have a monopoly. There is no price competition and there is a Pharmaceutical Manufacturers Association of Canada. Fifty-seven companies were members of it but the number has been reduced to 56. They manufacture 85 per cent of the drugs sold by prescription across Canada today. This bill makes an excellent start, may I say, in the direction of ridding the country of this monopoly. Drugs, to my way of thinking, are to make people well, not to make purses full.
I have in my hand a book written by Mr. Bill Stevenson. He discusses and exposes some of the unusual drug costs and prices in Canada today. He says that drug profits run as high as 26,000 to 28,000 per cent. Personally, in my investigations I have not come across drugs which carry such high profits, though I have come across drugs that have been marked up 9,700 per cent. I wish to indicate how this matter was referred to by Dr. William M. Wigle of Ottawa, President of the Pharmaceutical Manufacturers Association of Canada. Addressing a meeting he said:
I do not believe that the Canadian people are willing to jeopardize the future of the drug industry in Canada and that of its 10,000 employees for a will-o'-the-wisp profit which would put Canada at the mercy of foreign nations in the event of world-wide epidemics.
Is a 28,000 per cent profit a will-o'-the-wisp? I should hate to see a large profit in the drug industry.
The P.M.A.C. has been constantly present at committee meetings in one way or another since June, 1966. They appeared before the committee four times. They attended all committee meetings because they were afraid of what might be said. They fed questions to members of the committee and since then have been pressuring us with submissions and briefs, being afraid that some of their monstrous profits might be lost.
These members of the P.M.A.C. are the high profit boys. They are the monopolistic

members of, if you will forgive the expression, a smug minority which uses the word "freedom" in the sense that they are free to fleece the sick out of every last cent they can wring from them. The fact that a man is sick does not matter except that he is then a more vulnerable target for the industry's high pressure methods. To the members of the P.M.A.C., illness is their most valuable asset and they are capable, 85 per cent of the time, of conning the doctor to act as an agent to sell their products for them. So naturally they do not take kindly to a bill that is going to incapacitate this golden egg layer.
One brief that we received, Mr. Speaker, contained a comparison of generic and patent drugs. Ostensibly the brief did not come from the P.M.A.C., though you could smell where it came from as it came into the office. The independent survey we received claimed that basically there was no difference in cost between drugs prescribed under their generic names and those described by brand names. The people doing the survey selected their own group of drugs; there were 11 comparisons, I believe. Of those, two involved drugs that were brand name drugs which were cheaper than generic drugs. Actually, these so-called brand name drugs originally had been generic drugs but had been labelled with the manufacturer's label. The drugs that were selected for the comparison were, as I said, carefully selected. The intention was to show that certain generic drugs were more expensive than brand name drugs.
Those presenting the brief also misrepresented the situation by forgetting to refer to how drugs are sold. When a prescription is presented to a druggist, since he operates by charging a percentage profit, naturally the more expensive the original drug is the higher his profit will be. The way drugs are sold is interesting. The best prices at which drugs are obtained are when they are bought by stock lots which, for instance, may involve 100 bottles or 50 tablets and so on. If smaller amounts are bought, if 24, 20, or odd numbers of capsules or tablets are prescribed, the price charged is known as the breakdown price which may be higher than the stock lot price. The brief made unfair comparisons by attempting to compare stock lot prices with breakdown prices.
The suggestion was also made in the brief that the difference in cost between drugs prescribed under generic names compared with
February 12, 1968	COMMONS
brand names was of no important consequence. That is very interesting because I want to know to whom it is of no consequence. Did the brief mean it was of no consequence to the people of this country or to the P.M.A.C. boys?
I did some research into the cost of generic and brand name drugs in Ottawa. I investigated the drugs that had been mentioned and I found that in stock lots the generic drugs came to $52.30 and the brand name drugs came to $143.10. These prices were being charged for large quantities of drugs. Making inquiries about smaller quantities from the same druggist, I discovered that the generic drugs would have been sold at $28.50 and the brand names would have come to $51.15. Even allowing for any unfairness, if they say this is an inconsequential difference when in fact, according to their own selection of figures, it is almost double I maintain they were trying to misrepresent things when they brought this brief to the committee.
[DOT] (5:50 p.m.)
Possibly they were not satisfied with that brief as a demonstration of what they could do because they submitted a brief in their own name. This brief, like all the others, complained that they were even now being deprived of profits which they might have gained had they been given proper protection. The hon. member who spoke earlier quoted from the same paragraph as one I have marked here, containing a reference to companies A and B and to compulsory licensing.
I was interested in the statement it contains to the effect that the royalty the commissioner of patents gives to company A which initiates an invention is only a pittance. The hon. member did not explain why it is a pittance. It is a pittance because the royalty paid is based upon the cost of the manufacture of drugs, and the cost of manufacture bears no relation whatsoever to the selling price. This is why companies do not want compulsory licensing. Most companies, having made a fabulous profit on these drugs, then concede a voluntary licence after which they receive a royalty which they themselves designate. The company which receives it sells the product at a slightly lower cost. It does not have the advantage of the original patent name, but it pays a royalty to the mother company, the discovering company.
These are the people who are twisting these figures and making themselves appear as though they were the friends of the sick and

Patent Act-Trade Marks Act the elderly. Sometimes their protestations would bring tears to our eyes if we did not trouble to look at the facts of the situation. They complain about the importation of drugs under compulsory licence. Yet they themselves do this all the time in the case of patent drugs manufactured by United States parent companies. Most of the patent drugs manufactured in Canada are in actual fact manufactured by parent companies in the United States and shipped to Canada in dosage form. Here in Canada the subsidiaries bottle and label them and then have the dignity of being called drug manufacturers. So this patent arrangement amounts to another magic formula in favour of those who are capitalizing on illness and establishing a market for themselves by convincing others that not only do they need drugs but they need drugs with brand names only. They set out to brainwash doctors not only into prescribing their patented drugs but into prescribing drugs which in many cases patients do not really need-and drugs of a brand in whose selection doctors have no choice.
This establishes a pretty good market. Who has built up this market and built up these excess profits if it is not the P.M.A.C. itself? Even the Canadian Medical Association has been partly convinced, though I think this has been done with a certain amount of reticence. I believe the manufacturers have brought enough pressure to bear on the C.M.A. to convince many of its members that the present system is the only way in which drugs can be prescribed.
One of the well established habits of the P.M.A.C. is to disparage generic drugs both in the press and in doctors' offices, hoping to influence not only the doctors but the patients receiving care. In the brief to which I have just referred they speak of reputation as though it were holy ground and as though they have an exclusive claim on it. But there are many reputable firms which manufacture drugs under generic names.
The sales tax was recently removed and this should, of course, have caused the price of drugs to fall. This actually happened temporarily, at least, as the minister said. However, I am reliably informed that Parke, Davis are raising their prices and I am afraid this will undo all the good that the removal of the sales tax achieved.
I should like now to read into the record part of a column by Mr. D. H. Fullerton which appeared in the Calgary Albertan. This
February 12, 1968

Patent Act-Trade Marks Act article brings to light some of the lobbying and the pressures to which we have all been subject. The writer says:
In a society where the high cost of drugs is borne by those least able to afford it-the old, the sick and the poor-one may be pardoned for asking why action on drugs has not had a higher priority. One answer is being observed in Ottawa today where the well-heeled, monopolistic, and internally powerful drug industry has been recently mounting the most intensive lobby ever seen in the capital.

Later the article states:
Yet the shocking fact that even these mild measures to introduce some competition into the industry are assailed by the manufacturers suggests there is not much point in trying to apply a cosmetic approach to an industry with so little awareness of its public responsibility.
