Mr. Speaker, it is my honour to participate in the debate. Tonight I wish to do so as the ex-chairman of the special committee on drug costs and prices, to which reference has been made during this debate. I would like to put on the record the terms of reference of the committee, which were as follows:
That the committee be empowered to consider and recommend, as it may deem expedient, respecting a comprehensive and effective program to reduce the price of drugs.
As the house is aware, the committee reported on April 3, 1967 after over one year of intensive and detailed study. I think the basic feeling of the majority of the committee was that if we were to make recommendations which were to be taken seriously by the government, these recommendations had to be based on fact, and I believe we accomplished that. While many people have disagreed with our conclusions and recommendations, to my knowledge no one has challenged the material in the report on which these conclusions were based. I should like to remind the house that this was the unanimous report of a committee of the House of Commons composed of members from every political party in the house.
DEBATES	6647
Patent Act-Trade Marks Act
I would remind the house that there was no mention in the terms of reference to the matter of safety or quality of drugs. I am sure hon. members are aware that two years previous to that time a committee of the house had dealt in considerable detail with drug safety. The present committee realized that the question of costs could not be completely separated from that of safety. The actual cost of safety or quality control cannot be segregated from ordinary manufacturing costs, as they are often an integral part of the manufacturing process in any industry, whether it be a pharmaceutical or any other product. In any event, the committee found the actual cost of safety or quality control to be small but very essential. I would emphasize to the house that no recommendations of this committee would reduce the money spent on safety. As a matter of fact, the matter of safety must come before that of cost. After all, life is more important than money, and no recommendation of our committee should be carried out unless safety can be assured as much as possible.
We all know that the complete safety of any drug cannot be guaranteed, no matter how minor the drug or how major the government's caution and concern. As a matter of fact, if I were to summarize the report of the committee, I would say that the majority of the recommendations, by actual count 20 out of 23, fell into two major categories: first, those that were intended to make lower cost drugs available in Canada and, second, those that would ensure as much as practicable that these lower cost drugs would be safe for the use of the consumer.
[DOT] (8:40 p.m.)
I should like to review a few of the conclusions of the report and make a few comments on them. The first one I should like to comment upon is that no significant change has taken place in the drug cost structure since the recommendations of the Hall commission, which were primarily based upon the recommendations of the Restrictive Trade Practices Commission. So far as the committee could see, the drug industry had made no attempt to reduce drug costs, despite those reports which were very critical of the drug industry. The drug industry had not taken the report seriously and apparently had never expected the government to take any further action on that report, or on our report.
As has been mentioned before, there exists no single method or simple approach which
February 12, 1968

Patent Act-Trade Marks Act can be taken to reduce the price of drugs to the consumer. It was therefore necessary to present a series of recommendations to effect this purpose. As hon. members are aware, and as the minister said, the federal sales tax has been removed and some changes have been made in tariffs. This bill No. C-190 deals with another series of recommendations our committee made.
The medical profession, of course, is responsible for prescribing most drugs. If these committee recommendations are to be fully effective, the medical profession must be completely assured by the food and drug directorate of the safety of all drugs. If the medical practitioners in Canada cannot be assured that drugs in Canada are as safe, and I mean "safe" in a reasonable manner as human effort can reasonably make them, and are, therefore, prepared to use the lower priced drugs, then the report we submitted and the minister's proposed legislation is not worth the paper it is printed on. This legislation will be of no benefit to anyone unless the medical practitioners in Canada can be assured that the drugs that would be available under the minister's legislation would be safe for them to use.
The next conclusion concerns the implementation of the recommendation in connection with marketing and promotional expenses, and the reduction of excessive profits. As an example, the committee was greatly concerned with the average expenditure of 30 per cent of the manufacturer's dollar on promotion and marketing as opposed to 7 per cent being spent on research. In other words, more than four times as much money was being spent on marketing and advertising a drug as was being spent on research into medicinal products. As the hon. member for Hamilton South (Mr. Howe) said, it is important to know also that a good deal of the 7 per cent spent on research was spent on applied research, applying the benefits of other forms of research. Only a very small proportion of that was spent on basic medical research. The committee realized that the implementation of our recommendations could alter, in some respects, the form of the drug industry as it exists in Canada today, removing inefficiency and increasing competition. What the committee felt must be done is to introduce competition into the drug industry, not product competition such as duplication of another successful product which increases cost, but competition on prices, which is the kind that is needed in the drug industry.

I should like to say in passing that many countries, including the United States and the United Kingdom, are having a series of studies made of this problem. It is interesting to note in passing that the Sainsbury report in the United Kingdom recently recommended abolishing trade names and using only generic names for drugs.
I should like to talk for a few minutes about one of the major recommendations of the committee, namely that the food and drug directorate publish not less than once a month an informative bulletin to the medical profession giving complete details on drugs and their actions, and reviewing major drug usage in Canada. This would of course go not only to the medical profession but also to the related professions including pharmacy. The committee realizes that to ask a doctor to change his prescribing habits is a very serious responsibility. It should be done only if the doctor can be assured that the drugs he has the option of prescribing are as safe as possible. To do this the doctor should, and indeed must, have free access to a non-biased current report on drugs which would include certain data-and I should like to emphasize the words "non-biased". In other words, the bulletin would not be put out by a drug company and would be available free to the medical profession. The committee felt the following should be included in that bulletin:
1.	The generic name of the drug.
2.	Names of all manufacturers of the drug, and brand names of the drug.
3.	Comparative costs and clinical effectiveness of the drug.
4.	How the drug works; side effects, contraindications and toxicity.
5.	The last assay for each company's prod-duct, of content and availability of active ingredient, solubility and disintegration.
6.	Any problems with any company's product such as toxicity, impurity, seizures, court actions failure to meet food and drug directorate standards.
The committee feels that the food and drug directorate has been keeping some of its activities from the medical profession. The findings on drugs should be openly reported to the medical profession in public documents. If there are poor quality drugs on the market, then the medical and pharmaceutical professions should be told. The medical and related professions have to be convinced that
February 12, 1968

the food and drug directorate has full and accurate knowledge of the drug industry. To do this, they have to report fully and I believe, in a public bulletin. If the medical profession cannot be assured by giving them freely full and unbiased evidence of all the factors concerning drugs, then it is obvious we cannot expect the medical profession to change their prescribing habits in favour of the lower cost drugs.
I have been asked in what way this might tend to lower the price of drugs. Certainly, the staff that would be required by the food and drug directorate to publish such a bulletin would be expensive and would probably take up to two years to set into motion. I believe, however, that the savings that could be made if the medical profession used this bulletin to their own advantage, and more particularly to their patients' advantage, would be very substantial. The consumer would benefit greatly from this saving, enough to more than justify the expense.
Many hon. members here are aware of the large savings that can be made, many of which have been referred to today, when drugs are purchased under a tendering system. Most of these drugs do come from generic manufacturing houses. Many generic drugs are used by the staffs of various hospitals. These same staff doctors may not use generic drugs outside their hospital practice, but many are often doing so inside the hospital without being fully aware of the source of the medication they are prescribing.
I am convinced more doctors would prescribe the lower cost drugs of generic manufacturers if they were convinced that they were safe to use and equally effective. I hope therefore that the government will see fit, in the very near future, following these recommendations, to introduce the type of bulletin to which the committee made reference. Obviously the federal government has no power to implement some of the recommendations of our committee. Some of the recommendations come under the jurisdiction of provincial governments and some come under the heads of pharmaceutical bodies and other public bodies. I hope all those interested bodies will see to it that the recommendations are given serious consideration. Obviously the government cannot implement in a field in which it has no jurisdiction; we can only bring in recommendations. For instance, we have no control over the field of retail pharmacy, and therefore the government can make no recommendations in that area.

The unanimous conclusion-I emphasize the word "unanimous"-not only of the special committee on drug costs and prices but of the various other inquiries in Canada is that drug prices are higher than they need be and certainly higher than the public is prepared to pay without question. One of the major causes of drug costs has been attributed to the degree of protection accorded to the drug manufacturing industry by such laws as the Patent Act and the Trade Marks Act. This has resulted in a lack of competition. What the committee hopes the recommendation will accomplish is the injection of a greater degree of competition in the pharmaceutical industry at all levels. Despite the many studies that have taken place over the past ten years the industry has not, as far as I am aware, made any attempt to produce solutions to the problems. As I have said, Mr. Speaker, the government has removed the federal sales tax and has made changes in some of the various laws. Today's move is to bring in recommendations that change the patent and trade marks laws in such a way as to provide Canadians with less expensive but equally safe drugs.
There has been a great deal of discussion about patents and patent protection. I should like to point out to the house that patent protection at the present time in Canada is for 17 years and that the present legislation will not change it. The system of compulsory licensing that we are talking about has actually been in effect since 1923. The principle that food and drugs are different from other inventions was actually established in 1923, and is not being established now.
As far as compulsory licences are concerned, Mr. Speaker, I should like to quote the report of the special committee of the House of Commons on drug costs and prices. At page 38 appears this paragraph:
The committee found that up to 1949 no applications for compulsory licences had been made in Canada.
As I have said, Mr. Speaker, this was included in the legislation in 1923.

Those figures were as of September, 1966. The system of compulsory licensing has been

As the minister mentioned previously, patents in Canada-at least those relating to drugs-are now over 95 per cent foreign owned. Patent rights, despite this legislation, will be retained; and I do not believe that there will be any international implications of the kind several hon. members of the house alluded to during the debate.
As I have said, compulsory licensing has been the practice in Canada since 1923. It is also a system that is used in the United Kingdom under very similar legislation. To my knowledge, no one in the United Kingdom or in Canada has ever complained on an international level that the compulsory licensing system interfered with their patent rights, to their great detriment.
Some reference has been made to some literature that all of us have received during the last few days, particularly to a letter and a brief forwarded to various members of the house by P.M.A.C., the Pharmaceutical Manufacturers Association of Canada. The second paragraph of the letter reads:

Then it goes on:
We believe it might set an unfortunate precedent.
I have just pointed out to the house, Mr. Speaker, that this is not so. First of all, it would not abolish normal patent protection; nor would it set a precedent. The precedent was actually set in 1923.
In the third paragraph of their letter the association say that they had hoped there might be consultation on this legislation prior to its introduction. This legislation was introduced almost a year after the recommendations of our committee. The Pharmaceutical Manufacturers Association of Canada had the advantage of making many representations to the committee. Since that time the minister's office has been open to them for representations, and the minister has seen representatives of the association as a body on at least two occasions. He has also seen representatives of any drug company that wished to see him regarding the legislation, and has seen them, as far as I am aware, to the fullest of their wishes. While I am talking about the Pharmaceutical Manufacturers Association of Canada, Mr. Speaker, I should also like to disagree with a statement that was made in Florida by the president of the association. He stated that the Canadian parliamentary committee was willing to put Canada at the mercy of foreign nations in the event of world wide epidemics.
I am not sure how I should qualify this statement. Whether the changes in the legislation with regard to compulsory licensing go through or not, this statement could perhaps be said basically to be true. As was pointed out this afternoon, Canada does not have a significant, basic fine chemical industry. I might point out that the basic chemicals used by the drug industry in Canada today do not originate in Canada, but come mainly from the United States. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, if the statement to which I have referred is true after the legislation passes, then it is equally true before the legislation passes.
I also think the house should understand that under the laws and regulations of the food and drug directorate at least a five-year monopoly is given to any company that introduces a new drug into Canada under the principle of patent protection. This is because a drug that comes into Canada under a patent protection is classified as a new drug until it satisfies the directorate that the company has met their requirements concerning research on the particular drug in question.
The minimum period of time that elapses before a drug loses its new drug status is five years, and usually is a great deal longer than that. In other words, the company that produces the drug does indeed have a five-year monopoly, during which time it may regain its research costs and can actually go out and try to corner the market for that particular product. The company has five years' access to a completely monopolized market; and as I have said, Mr. Speaker, usually the period is more than five years.
No company, Mr. Speaker, has asked or is likely to ask for a compulsory licence before new drug status is lost. If it does this, it means that it has to reduplicate all the investigational work on the particular drug. No compulsory licence has ever been applied for by a company while that stipulation was there. It is a very expensive procedure to introduce a new drug. Therefore I think it very unlikely that a compulsory licence would be asked for during that time. So there is no question, Mr. Speaker, that the major
February 12, 1968
patent rights are retained, and certainly a complete monopoly without any risk of compulsory licence is available to the company for at least five, and perhaps many more years.
There is no question that patents do influence the price of drugs. I think reference was made to the fact that the United States, does not have a compulsory licensing system, as we have in Canada. Chloromycetin was much cheaper in Canada under our compulsory licensing system than it was in the United States. Mr. Speaker, we listened at great length this afternoon to the minister, and this evening to the chairman of the special committee on drug costs in Canada, and other related matters. It has been enlightening and informative I am sure to those members of the house who were not on the committee, but I must say frankly that sitting here this afternoon I was not at all sure I was a member of that committee.
My remarks will centre largely on what I consider to be a serious misreading of the intentions of the bulk of the recommendations of the special committee. The purpose of the

February 12, 19S8
study and, I suppose, the intent of the bill- the two may be compatible at this early point- was to allow compulsory licences for the importation of prescription drugs in finished dosage form. The spin-off was intended to encourage competition at the manufacturers level, and thereby reduce the cost of drugs. As a proposition, this seems valid on the surface, but it must be considered in the light of an imporan word which has been loosely used by some hon. members m this debate so far. That word is "safety". We on this side agree with the intent of any measure which will lower the prices of prescription drugs to consumers. This is a philosophy to which I think everyone in this house adheres. In saying this we do not mean to imply either directly or otherwise that the cost of drugs in Canada is necessarily too high. Indeed I directed questions to a large number of witnesses who appeared before the committee on that specific point-as to whether in their opinion the cost of drugs in Canada was too high. The generality of opinion was that they might be high, but that they were not necessarily too high.
We started this inquiry on February 15, 1966 when a special committee was set up. It is not necessary to review the terms of reference in detail, but I will emphasize one point because it is an essential part of the background to the remarks I intend to make. We were not asked to say whether prices were too low or too high. Rather we were directed to find a comprehensive and effective program to reduce the price of drugs in Canada, the inference being that the price of drugs was, in fact, too high. As the chairman of the special committee has correctly pointed out, we were not necessarily to concern ourselves about safety. To tackle these terms of reference realistically we had to make some basic decisions at the outset. Most of these are clearly set out, and they are to be found at page 6 of the committee's final report to the house. They are, in essence, that the committee's conclusions should be such that any of its recommendations, if adopted, should continue to maintain a proper balance between industry and consumer, and take into consideration the importance of continued and increased scientific research in Canada.
This was the fundamental premise from which we started. No recommendation could be considered which, although designed to lower drug prices in Canada, might produce

Patent Act-Trade Marks Act drugs of questionable safety or have a detrimental effect on other aspects of the Canadian economy. We were given our terms of reference and we set our guide lines. The committee met some 63 times. We heard evidence from firms, associations, private individuals, government agencies and governments. In addition we had before us the research studies which have been mentioned -the findings of three previous Canadian commissions, those of the royal commission on health services, the patents, copyright and industrial designs commission, which was the Ilsley commission of 1960 and the Restrictive Trade Practices Commission. We also had access to many other reports and texts in this field such as the Kefauver report, which has been mentioned today, the Hinch-cliffe report from the United Kingdom, published in 1959, and the reports of several Canadian provinces-Manitoba, British Columbia and Ontario. Not least, I suggest, we had before us the reports of the Boyd and Hilliard committees, both appointed under the aegis of the present government. These I suggest are the ones most pertinent to what we are about to do here some time during the next day or so.
I mention this background to illustrate the concern which has existed for some time not only in Canada but in other countries in connection with the drug industry, and to show that the Harley committee approached the task assigned to it with a full awareness of its responsibility to fellow members in the house and to all Canadians.
We on this side believe that the report generally represented an adequate and proper discharge of that responsibility. Before we look closely at the bill before us I believe we should refresh our collective memories as to the recommendations of the special committee on drug prices and costs and the implications of the implementation of those recommendations. I should like to read at least three of the committee's conclusions, because I think they are germane to the conclusions at whicn we on this side believe the house should arrive. The first is:
That the food and drug directorate publish not less than once a month an informative bulletin to the medical profession giving complete details on drugs and their actions and reviewing major drug uses in Canada.
Notwithstanding the comments of the previous speaker, I would ask the minister whether this has been done. Has it been done

Patent Act-Trade Marks Act yet? Has any action been taken to lead to the implementation of this particular recommendation? The minister admitted earlier today that it had not.

That present ministerial authority as provided in Section 38 of the Customs Act be amended in so far as the importation of drugs into Canada is concerned, and that future value for duty be set in all cases at the cost of production of the imported drug plus an allowance for gross profit (ie. an allowance to cover the actual manufacturer's administrative overhead, selling costs and net profit, etc.)

Here again I should like to ask the minister what has been done about this. It has been indicated that there has been a narrowing of the area in respect of the fifth conclusion, which states that the Customs Act should be amended to make clear that dumping duties with respect to drugs be limited only to affect those drugs of a kind made in Canada. I should like to ask the minister to tell us what the narrowing has been, or where the protection is. So far as I have been able to determine, this information is not available to us in print. I do not particularly wish to discuss all the recommendations, but I mention these three because they are indicative of the situation.
Some considerable time has elapsed since the publication of this report. The government has acted on one or two of the ideas set out here and has embodied them in at least one clause of the bill. However, the lack of action on the part of the government is indicative of the fact that there has been a rejection by government officials of the report of the special committee. Indeed, most of the provisos attached to the recommendations of the special committee have been dropped. Of the seven recommendations of the committee which are pertinent to Bill No. C-190-recommendations 2, 11, 17, 18, 19, 20 and 21 we find that only one, recommendation 21, was actually implemented, and that only two additional ideas were picked up and used in another form. This is the situation, in our opinion and I believe in the opinion of most members who were members of the special committee-in spite of the fact that the recommendations in the report are spelled out clearly, and in spite of the fact that drug prices in Canada are indeed higher than they need be.


According to Mr. David Henry, the reasons for these prices are not single but are multiple and relate not only to the pharmaceutical manufacturing companies but also to the retail pharmacies and indeed, as we all know, the taxation policies of the government. They are due, as well, to the food and drug directorate, because of the regulations it imposes on the industry, the drug wholesalers, the physician who prescribes the drug and indeed the person who must have recourse to the drug and demands the very best. If I were a doctor I suppose it would be simple for me to say, "How often do we in this discipline hear workers say that they cannot afford to stay off work, and ask whether there is some pill or shot that will fix them up so that they may be able to stay on the job."
The recommendations of the committee also pointed out very clearly the importance that should attach to the matter of safety and the vital role of the food and drug directorate in this regard. They also point out the need for more research in Canada, both in the pharmaceutical and medical fields. As a member of the committee I am very gratified at the manner in which the pharmaceutical manufacturing industry and the retail pharmacists have responded to and have implemented certain committee recommendations. We see that the pharmaceutical associations across Canada are considering, and I think perhaps one province, if not more, has already instituted, recommendation No. 15 of the committee which deals with the ethics of the profession or the discipline of pharmacy. This has to do with the method of determining drug prices to the consumer.
The method of pricing drugs and some of the other recommendations have at least been given active consideration by the retail pharmacists and pharmaceutical associations. Members on this side of the house find encouraging the co-operation which has already begun to evolve between the manufacturers and the wholesalers in respect of the abolition of the recommended price lists. I believe stringent steps have been taken to revise their promotional practices. This was another of our recommendations.
This afternoon and evening we have had discussions about this being the reason for one of the highest costs in the manufacturing dollar. Something must be done in this regard. It is not a matter of a recommendation having been made, and ignored by the industry.

I should like to ask again what the government has done in this regard. Let us take a look at what has been done. The government has removed the inequitable sales tax on drugs. Indeed I wonder why it ever should have been increased to the level of 12 per cent. The grants to the Medical Research Council have been increased. This was mentioned earlier, and I believe everyone is gratified that this has been done. But what about the food and drug directorate itself? There was a good deal of evidence which pointed out the need for increased staff and the inability of the food and drug directorate to actively meet its commitments with its present staff. I suppose I should ask whether the personnel and facilities have been expanded, or indeed whether the recommendations of the Hilliard committee have been implemented.
The report of the Hilliard committee and the report of the Boyd committee were considered to be very important reports. They deal with the matter of the safety of drugs. I suggest that the government in this regard has procrastinated and delayed, and I believe this has been done deliberately. I ask again whether the Tariff Board has reviewed the drug tariff structure pursuant to recommendation No. 6 in the committee report. This is the recommendation which asks that the federal government instruct the Tariff Board to review the drug tariff structure. Has this been done and, if not, why not? Has the Customs Act been amended in line with recommendation No. 5 which I read into the record a while ago? Again we have the vague assurance that there has been a narrowing in this particular regard. We have had nothing specific. I suggest that the answer by the government in respect of these questions is Bill No. C-190, despite the warnings and recommendations contained in the committee report and despite conclusion No. 3, which deals with the matter of the issuance of a bulletin by the government.
The government has wilfully ignored the recommendations of the special committee. The result is that we have Bill C-190. We know it proposes simply to grant the commissioner of patents the full power to grant licences under patents relating to medicines, and to grant licences for the importation of medicines in any form. No reference to safety is made in the bill. There is absolutely nothing in respect of guarantees. Apparently the minister and his government are so intent on
Patent Act-Trade Marks Act reducing the prices of drugs they do not care what kind of drugs are imported, so long as they are cheaper. It is not good enough for us on this side of the house or for the Canadian people to save a few pennies, without measuring value and the safety of the users of the drug. Surely that is poor business sense.
Hon. members of this house should be aware of the incalculable harm and danger we would do if we did not bring to the attention of all members and the Canadian people the dangers implicit in this bill. We would be abdicating our responsibility to all Canadians if we did not object to it as vigourously as possible. We would be failing in our duty if we accepted any bill that puts price ahead of the well-being of the people of the country, and we know instinctively that this is a bad bill.
This whole question of safety was raised and dealt with repeatedly throughout the hearings of the committee.

I mention the physician merely so that it will be borne in mind that no matter how much opportunity for price competition may be made available, unless a physician has confidence in the source of the drug and in the measures taken to ensure the purity, safety and effectiveness of the product he would not prescribe it for his patient. We heard evidence before the committee as well on the question of drugs coming into the country, and we heard evidence of the inability of the food and drug directorate to check effectively on the various factors involved in ensuring absolute safety of drugs. Indeed, if my general understanding is accurate, the concern of the food and drug directorate is that a particular drug should measure up to what it is represented to be. We have all read very recently about the sale of water to Viet Nam under the guise of its being a drug. If it can happen in one country it can happen in another. I suppose as long as it was listed as water the food and drug directorate would not object.
Let me again quote from page 2167 of this evidence taken before the committee. Perhaps I should not quote this, as it is quite lengthy, but it has reference to what Dr. Hilliard had to say.
In spite of all these facts the minister continues to ignore the advice of a series of dedicated Canadians, both from the public service and the industrial level. I wonder sometimes whether the minister's common sense has been affected by more heady prospects which might lie ahead. I am wondering if he is not more concerned about his stance before the conference to be held in this city in a few weeks. He has continued to ignore these remarks and recommendations, contained not only in the conclusions of the special committee but in other evidence available to us and available to the government.

This is a very serious matter. The government suggests that there is adequate protection in respect of drugs coming into the country. Here is an example of where the purchasing agent did not even know the origins of the drugs he was ordering. They could indeed have come from the same source which supplied the salt water to Viet Nam. I suggest that the issue is quite apparent. It does not seem to us that the government is at all concerned with safety.
I do not know whether deliberately or due to a lack of knowledge they have left this matter out of Bill C-190 entirely. There has been ample persuasion to suggest to the minister and his departmental officials that indeed you cannot separate them. As I say, Mr. Speaker, I am not sure what has been the motivation of the government.
Many areas should have been touched on and I hope will be touched on arising out of the effects of the implementation of the plan as outlined by the minister before the committee. For example, we had a great deal of evidence which indicated that the importation of drugs in the manner suggested would lead to the destruction of the pharmaceutical industry in Canada. That was not simply the pleading of a special interest.
We heard earlier in the day that there was nothing that would encourage expansion by the small manufacturer. I fail to see anything so far in what the minister or anybody else has said that would justify the industry remaining in this country at all. Why should it stay here and operate at the high cost levels of the economic structures in Canada today, when there are many areas where the economic structures are much more compatible with this type of industry? This is the type of industry where transportation is not a major factor.
In this connection, Mr. Speaker, Mr. Henry stated in the committee that there were grave doubts held by his department whether it is a good idea to have a pharmaceutical industry in Canada at all. I think he perhaps phrased it in a way to suggest that, as far as the industry is concerned, we must look at the situation very carefully to see whether it would be advisable to continue the industry in this country. I cannot in any way see anything to reject that statement as a premise.

Mr. Speaker, I listened with interest to the remarks of the previous speaker, and in the time at my disposal I would like to deal with some of the objections to the bill that have been raised by the vested interests and by hon. gentleman opposite, which seemed to have some similarities.
It would seem that the main thesis propounded by the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Forrestall) in opposition to this bill was not based on the fact that he feels the cost of drugs is unreasonable. I think he raised two points in objection to the bill. It would appear that in his mind the objections were so great as to permit what is an intolerable situation to exist for some time. Therefore if we are to decide on the merits of the hon. member's speech, we must reflect on the objections he has raised. His major objection had to do with safety. The drug industry itself has made reference to safety and quality control, and there is no question that this is a matter which can arouse a considerable amount of emotional support. It is entirely consistent in the art of politics, when advocating a course of action which in all other respects may be undesirable and unpopular, to try to And one aspect of your case which arouses public sympathy, and by doing that perhaps to obscure the major merits of your opponent's argument, thus helping to win the day on fallacious grounds. I believe that if the arguments of the hon. member opposite and the drug industry were to carry the day, the Canadian people would be done a considerable disservice.
I do not want to spend a great deal of time on the matter of the safety of drugs, because it has already been dealt with eloquently by previous speakers and by the interjection of

the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow). The hon. member for Halifax said he saw no mention of this in the bill. May I refer him to subclause 13 which requires that notice be given to the Department of National Health and Welfare; and it is surely the function of the food and drug directorate to determine the safety and quality of drugs. There is nothing in the training of a patent officer and nothing to qualify that branch of government permitting it to set the criteria for safety.
The suggestion has been made by the drug industry and by the hon. member for Halifax that there is a relationship between patents and safety, and patents and quality control, and that any change in the patent law goes to the root of the problem of safety and quality control, when in fact the large body of evidence collected by the Hall commission and by the committee of the house shows the contrary. Notwithstanding that evidence and the provisions in this legislation, both the drug industry and the hon. member for Halifax have placed emphasis on the safety issue. Were I one who wanted to oppose the bill, were I not greatly concerned about the cost of drugs, and were I looking for arguments which might have some popular appeal for the general public which might not have the opportunity to examine the matter closely, quite obviously the issue to choose would be safety and quality control. It is an excellent technique which is as old as the art of politics itself.
In this case, however, the arguments of the hon. member opposite have little or no resemblance to the facts, which is what this chamber is concerned about. Naturally we are all concerned about the matter of safety and quality control. I think it would be ridiculous to assume that the royal commission on health services, the standing committee of the house, and the two doctors, members of the house, who spoke in this debate could, on the one hand be concerned about the price of drugs and on the other not be concerned about safety and quality control. Quite obviously they are concerned about both. I think that if you can get away with it, it is a quite admirable technique to try to confuse the issue. I hope that all hon. members have seen through this technique of the drug industry and of the hon. member for Halifax, who would appear to have presented the same arguments to the house that many of us have heard from the drug industry.
